Matched 2×2 cong/song–cou/sou diagnostic: retain within one error or all four readers, cross using pointer only for reader selection with also adding labelled lesson waveform to its nearest-example bank. Joint transfer/96 and retention/384: one-error selection only 39/300, plus example 36/294; all-reader selection only 55/293, plus example 51/292. Retaining all represented both replies 90/96. Reused placements, no new mastery evidence.

Matched correction ensemble diagnostic: majority of receipt-compatible readers, abstaining reader votes excluded, ties backed off to previous selector. One-error shortlist unchanged at 39/96 joint and 300/384 retention. With all four available, vote 47/96 joint vs single 55/96 (3 repairs, 11 losses), retention 299/384 vs 293/384. Retrospective panel, no promotion.

Matched second-voice clarification: preview remaining development voice saying the same clarified form, ask when surviving readers disagree, leave probes and untaught form untouched. Among 96 distinct pointer histories using all four readers, 36 extra pointers; joint transfer 60 vs 55 /96, established 299 vs 293 /384. One-error shortlist 48 vs 39 /96 and 302 vs 300 /384. Open retrospective cohort; preview costs not priced.

Second-voice economics, one correct untaught object choice = 1 unit, two future test uses per history. Reconstructing paired outcomes across 96 histories with 96 nominal previews and 36 labels: 11 errors repaired, 4 correct outputs lost, net +7/192 outputs. Queried histories 7 positive, 26 net zero, 3 negative. Break-even 96*preview_fee+36*label_fee=7, excluding compute, prior teaching, retention utility. Zero preview cost label ceiling 7/36.

Correction to second-voice economics: original selector already reused the first pointer in the second-vote check. Known-repeat no-second-label replay matches all 192 outcome/retention rows with zero additional labels. Prior 36 label fees are conditional protocol charges, not necessary information. Preview/audio remains necessary for the measured gain.

Serbian vocabulary pilot, four words selected by metadata coverage before scoring. Retrieved the frozen 24 clips from revision e115404d3dfce0c504d32c6803d0b93936bcf7c8 of Serbian Spoken Words and verified each speaker, word and sentence against the frozen selection. The pre-existing spectrum nearest-exemplar control scored 6/8 and 4/8 with one teaching example per word, then 7/8 and 5/8 with two. Same two probe blocks at both doses. Supplied word cuts; no independent localization or teaching-saving claim. Local per-item results in phonetic-foundation/serbian-pilot-spectrum.json.

Serbian pilot follow-up on the same 24 clips after the baseline was known. Sound-foundations 0.6.0 supplied detected event starts through the kernel; a separate consumer compared ordered segment spectra by dynamic time warping. Replacing the detected starts with equally spaced cuts preserved each clip's segment count. Detected starts scored 4/8 and 4/8 at one example per word, 7/8 and 3/8 at two. Equal spacing scored 4/8 and 4/8, then 5/8 and 3/8. Neither dose surpassed the original fixed-spectrum control overall. Supplied word endpoints, unlabelled interior starts, descriptive repeated probes. Raw receipts and decisions in serbian-kernel-units.json.

Connected-speech boundary diagnostic on the 32 locally cached replica utterances. Called the frozen boundaries operation once on each complete 8 kHz waveform. Matched predicted starts one-to-one within 20 ms of corpus-aligned phone starts, excluding spn/sil/sp and empty reference labels. Equal-spacing control preserved predicted count and the first/last detected times per utterance. By language (hits, control hits, reference count): Belarusian (44,25,205), Catalan (42,33,399), French (47,36,349), Swahili (54,35,319). Total 187/376 predictions matched, covering 187/1272 reference starts; control 129/376. These reused corpus alignments are an external timing reference, not independent human verification. Results in connected-kernel-boundary.json.

Prediction tested on the same 32 connected recordings: large local spectral changes inside the detected speech span would recover more missed starts than spending the same number of guesses on time alone. Fixed analysis used 12 log-power bands at 8 kHz, 20 ms spectral differences, 35 ms separation of added peaks, and about one extra candidate per 120 ms. All 1,272 aligned starts retained, including a recording without two detected endpoints. Of 1,166 combined predictions, 548 matched within 20 ms, against 432 with equally spaced additions and 453 with largest-gap-first additions. The original 376 predictions matched 187. Descriptive result on reused recordings; computed in the consumer, not installed as a new expert. Raw counts by recording in connected-boundary-flux.json.

Fixed spectral-change proposals tested for phone identification on 32 cached cv-pair utterances disjoint from the 32 boundary-development utterances. Previously used recordings, not a blind corpus. Kernel base starts plus spectral peaks or equally many largest-gap additions. Existing source-labelled spectral centroid reader excluded the evaluation language and evaluated speaker from its source bank. Read segment midpoints; require matching phone and onset within 20 ms, one-to-one. Of 745 eligible reference phones and 933 candidates per arm, peaks yielded 269 timing matches and 76 joint matches; gap placement yielded 200 and 53. Descriptive gain in joint recovery, low absolute coverage. Results in connected-boundary-ipa.json.

Timing-vs-naming fork: fixed 269 one-to-one onset matches by time alone before comparing ordinary and corpus-aligned midpoint readings on identical audio with the same reader. Ordinary 75 correct, aligned 90 correct; 25 rescued, 10 lost, 169 wrong under both, 65 correct under both. Ordinary midpoint fell within the reference span 232 times. Earlier 76 joint matches allowed label-specific pairing, so that count measures a different estimand. Most frequent aligned errors were k→n (11) and m→n (10). Files connected_boundary_midpoint.py and connected-boundary-midpoint-fork.json in the external research archive.

Aligned 14-phone diagnostic on the 741 previously evaluated occurrences. Kept the same source split and centroid classifier, excluding the target language and target speakers. Compared a 20 ms midpoint with first/middle/last 20 ms windows inside the annotated phone, either averaged or concatenated in temporal order. Correct totals 270, 257, 285 respectively. k→n errors 3, 1, 1 out of 68 k; m→n errors 8, 6, 6 out of 45 m. Both three-window readers reduced those specific confusions, so the reductions alone do not isolate an ordering effect. Per-occurrence data in cv-temporal-ipa.json. This diagnostic supplies the entire annotated interval and reuses an open benchmark.

Audio-derived-interval transfer of the three-window reader. Used 32 previously opened cv-fresh-order recordings, separate from the aligned cv-transition comparison. Matched kernel plus spectral-change proposals, 1,301 per arm. Among 687 eligible corpus-aligned phone occurrences, the timing-plus-identity totals were 122 for midpoint, 124 for three-window average, and 129 for ordered windows. Raw results in connected-temporal-ipa.json. This is a low-coverage diagnostic on reused audio with a source-labelled reader.

Fresh-speaker confirmation with the unchanged three readers and candidate detector. Pinned corpus revision a5ec8b8a289d09765551dc9d133a8a6daf400081. Excluded 109 speaker IDs found in archived CV row metadata and existing audio files; selected one recording per additional speaker before scoring. 41 voices, six languages. Joint onset and identity within 20 ms: midpoint 112, average 109, ordered 114 out of 950 eligible starts with 1,196 proposals per arm. No convincing replicated order advantage. Frozen placements and raw per-speaker counts in unheard-placements-0.json and unheard-temporal-ipa.json.

Post-confirmation level diagnostic, 41 fixed speakers. German raw: 36 candidates, only 4 onset matches and no joint matches across 47 eligible phones; two recordings produced one or zero candidates. Rescaling the 8 kHz proposal waveform to peak 0.9 while holding 16 kHz naming audio unchanged raised German onset matches to 25 and joint matches to 4 at 155 proposals. Across all six languages raw: 1196 proposals, 377 onset and 112 joint; normalized: 1708, 545 and 169. Uniformly thinning normalized candidates to at most the original count in each recording gave 1170, 378 and 106. Exploratory comparison on opened recordings. Full-utterance peak needs future samples and original count cap is a diagnostic; no online gain claimed. Raw files unheard-level-{raw,peak,capped}.json.

Bounded-lookahead consumer diagnostic on the opened 41-speaker cohort. Both rules emitted one candidate per complete 120 ms block, including silence. One placed it at 60 ms, the other selected the strongest 12-band spectral change inside the block. The same midpoint reader used the following candidate to close each interval. At exactly 1,891 naming calls per rule, spectral placement located 412/950 and jointly named 136/950; clock placement located 266 and jointly named 77. Paired speaker bootstrap (10,000 samples) joint recall difference +6.21 points, 95% interval +3.87 to +8.43. Matched candidate counts; extra front-end compute for spectral placement was not cost-matched. Offline replay; no package or live latency claim.

Installed sound-foundations 0.7.0 block-change via fresh wheel and generic kernel registration. Commit aafc812, 8 tests pass. All 1,891 block offsets equal the replay reference to the sample. Consumer verification surfaced float-rounding sensitivity in the old inclusive 20 ms evaluator; the corrected installed probe compares integer samples at 8 kHz. Latency measures kernel invocation in a warm process, excluding audio capture and block accumulation.

Downstream check of the installed 0.7.0 block-change operation on the frozen Serbian word pilot. Made 93 typed kernel calls across 24 clips. Same supplied word endpoints, one segment cut per complete 120 ms block, identical spectral segment measurements and nearest-exemplar dynamic time warping. After one example per word the expert scored 5/8 and 5/8, the clock 6/8 and 5/8. At two examples both scored 7/8 and 4/8 and agreed in correctness on every probe. Neither reached 85% on both blocks. No teaching reduction observed; doses reuse the same probes. External receipts and predictions in serbian-block-transfer.json.

Cross-speaker ABX diagnostic on the 41-voice cohort, supplied corpus phone intervals of at least 20 ms. Fixed one waveform token per speaker/phone by hash; A/B from one speaker and both X alternatives from another in the same language. Each eligible ordered speaker pair weighted equally within each contrast. Midpoint vs ordered 3-window accuracy: p/b .333/.583 (6 speaker pairs); t/d .520/.560 (50); m/n .527/.500 (94); t/k .530/.550 (100); i/u .716/.750 (116); a/i .860/.795 (132). Pairs share speakers, and phonetic neighbors were uncontrolled. No contrast reached 90%; this is a diagnostic of the spectral representations, without an IPA classifier. Raw decisions in unheard-abx.json.

Context-matched cross-voice ABX. Required both speakers to supply both consonants before exactly the same vowel in the same language; one hashed token per speaker/consonant/vowel. The 41-voice one-utterance cohort had zero qualifying pairs for m/n and t/k. On the separately scored broader audio archive, midpoint versus midpoint plus spectral differences across the consonant end and first 40 ms of the vowel: m/n 159/288 vs 164/288; t/k 204/400 vs 208/400. Ordered speaker pairs and reused tokens are dependent. These modest descriptive changes do not establish fresh-voice transfer. External results in adjacent-abx.json.

Fresh matched-context confirmation of frozen consonant cue comparison. Took first 16 eligible speaker IDs in each of pinned test shards 1 and 2, excluding prior CV row metadata speakers and the earlier 41 speakers. Loaded 64 recordings from 32 new speakers before scoring. Same eligibility and hash/token rule as archived ABX. For m/n, midpoint 16/24, transition 20/24; for t/k, 46/80 and 50/80. Ordered cross-speaker pairs reuse tokens; this small test cannot establish 90% cross-speaker mastery. External artifacts matched-new-speakers.json and matched-new-abx.json.

Additional contrast transfer cohort: same pinned revision, seven remaining shards, up to 16 first eligible speaker IDs per shard; excluded the earlier 32 and 41 speakers plus archived CV row metadata. 218 recordings, 60 new speakers. Same frozen waveform tokens, matched vowels and frozen spectral features. Midpoint vs transition for m/n: 18/32 vs 20/32; t/k: 17/36 vs 19/36. Pairs reuse speakers. Raw decisions by language and vowel in matched-transfer-abx.json.

Equal-label IPA comparison on the matched transfer corpus, reusing the same 20 ms midpoints and phone means. Source excluded target language and evaluation speakers. A shared within-phone covariance metric with fixed 10% isotropic shrinkage yielded 1,677/4,710 versus 1,716/4,710 for the original scaled Euclidean metric. Positive in Spanish and French, negative in Catalan, English and Swahili. Both readers use corpus intervals in training and evaluation; these are recognition diagnostics. Per-token outputs in matched-ipa-covariance.json.

Fixed acoustic-cue fork: append maximum normalized autocorrelation over 40–200 samples and zero-crossing rate to the same 20 ms spectrum. Same source labels, scaling and nearest centroid; held evaluation language/speakers out of fit. Corpus-supplied midpoint diagnostic: 1,845/4,710 vs 1,716/4,710 on the 60-speaker transfer cohort, with improvements in all five languages. On the separate previously opened 32-speaker Catalan cohort, 706/1,830 vs 622/1,830. This measures the two cues jointly and uses existing alignments. Raw per-token predictions in voicing-ipa-transfer.json and voicing-ipa-replica.json.

Fixed two voicing cues evaluated on self-placed intervals of the 41-speaker cohort. Same 1,891 offsets from installed block-change and same centroid training labels for both readers; gold phone intervals used only to score target speech. Baseline reproduced 148 of 950 jointly timed and named; adding periodicity and crossings produced 163. Speaker-paired bootstrap gain +1.58 points (95% +0.54 to +2.75). Audio already used for boundary diagnostics, separate speakers from aligned-cue comparisons. Per-utterance results in voicing-kernel-fork.json.

Sound-foundations 0.8.0 packages voicing-cues on a typed 320-sample 16 kHz mono frame. Fresh wheel installation, nine package tests passed. All 1,891 kernel-returned cue pairs matched the frozen reference within 1e-12. The 41-speaker replay reproduced the previous per-utterance results byte-for-byte and 163/950 joint identifications; this is implementation parity on the same data.

Serbian transfer of packaged voicing cues: fixed block-change cuts, 20 ms midpoint spectrum scaled from the non-Serbian source bank, identical nearest-exemplar DTW; augmented arm appends the two kernel-returned measurements. At one example per word, spectrum 5/8 and 6/8, augmented 6/8 and 6/8. At two examples both 7/8 and 4/8. Input is previously frozen word-cut 8 kHz audio resampled to 16 kHz for the measurement contract. Same test clips across doses, no durable 85% crossing. Raw data serbian-voicing-transfer.json.

Expanded Serbian acquisition test: 160 distinct sentence clips across four new words, with disjoint train/dev/test voice sets of 29/22/18. Excluded the pilot speakers. At each of four doses, two new balanced 16-clip blocks; ≥14/16 on each qualifies. Dense raw DTW first qualified at 4 examples/word, block-based augmented and directly supervised readers at 8, sparse spectrum and whole-word control unreached. Post-result density fork on identical placements: dense kernel voicing plus source-scaled spectrum scored 15/16 and 15/16 at one example/word, 12/16 and 14/16 at two, 15/16 and 16/16 at four. Dense scratch scored 11/16 and 13/16 at one. Exploratory crossing is non-monotonic and requires independent confirmation. No general teaching-saving claim. Clips have supplied word boundaries. Frozen inventory, placements, individual scores and density fork in phonetic-foundation/serbian-curve/.

Frozen dense voicing comparison on four additional Serbian words (pravo, rad, ljudi, vreme). New sentences, 160 clips across 26 teaching, 22 dev and 18 test voices, disjoint within this installation. At 1/2/4/8 examples per word scratch scored 10+11, 14+13, 14+13, 16+15 per two 16-clip blocks; dense voicing 12+10, 16+13, 14+14, 16+15. First qualifying doses: 4 vs 8, a 50% observed reduction on this vocabulary, by one correct decision on the second block at dose 4. Outcome remains sensitive to probe sampling. Sparse augmented crossed at 8, supervised sparse and whole-word controls did not cross. Frozen plan, results and warm kernel cue timing in serbian-confirm/.

Croatian transfer prediction before scoring: keep Serbian dense voicing features, scaling, DTW, doses and two-block threshold frozen. Compare against the prior dense scratch reader, dense scaled spectrum, sparse expert, whole-word and supervised sparse controls. Choose four words of at least four letters by speaker coverage only, excluding previously tested Serbian forms and named speakers. Expect the dense scratch control to be competitive. Count unreached cases and report first crossings with paired speaker resampling. Pinned datatab/croatian-spoken-words revision f3fad67cdc8f78472e341a8dcd60d46a863cb5cc; supplied word endpoints.

Croatian vocabulary result: applied a pre-score eligibility filter for enough distinct sentences to fill every block, then froze 160 placements from 78 speakers (28/25/25). At one example per word dense voicing scored 14/16 and 14/16, dense scratch 13/16 and 14/16. At two examples scratch first crossed (15/16 and 14/16); dense voicing 15/16 on both. At four both missed one block, at eight both passed again. Earlier observed crossing on this vocabulary depends on one probe at the first dose. Frozen plan, warm service timings, per-item guesses in croatian-confirm/.

Croatian cost replay: two separate local processes, cached 16 kHz word WAV files, generation-free case. Verified all 128 predictions per arm against saved guesses. One-time recomputation of augmented source scale used 697 labelled phone intervals from 32 recordings and 21 speakers in 1.37 s; this excludes upstream corpus annotation and earlier research. At the observed first threshold, augmented received 2.08 s of target training audio, scratch 3.70 s. At the identical one-example dose, p95 WAV-read-through-word-choice latency was 13.11 vs 6.08 ms on 32 probes. Hardware observations, not human annotation times. Per-call timings and process high-water RSS in croatian-confirm/{dense_aug,scratch}-cost.json.

Unlabelled-source calibration fork: use nonoverlapping 20 ms source frames with energy above 1% of each recording maximum, no reference to source phone spans or symbols. Scaled eight spectral and two installed voicing measurements using their pooled standard deviations. On identical probes the Croatian dense reader scored 14+14, 15+15, 14+16, 15+16; Serbian scored 11+10, 16+13, 15+14, 16+15. The earlier first crossings survive removing phone-directed source sampling. This is a diagnostic on opened vocabularies with supplied target word cuts, not independent replication. Frozen scales, frame counts and replay outputs archived.

Estonian transfer prediction before scoring: keep the unlabelled scale and 10 ms reader fixed. Compare with the same dense raw spectrum DTW and the existing matched controls on four new Estonian keywords chosen by speaker coverage in pinned MSWC metadata. Use deterministic speaker partition, disjoint source sentence recordings and the previous two-block threshold across 1/2/4/8 examples per word. Record unreached thresholds. Supplied aligned word clips are a distinct recording condition from the parliamentary corpora.

Estonian confirmation (MSWC CC BY 4.0, revision 0bc9df68e92fd6bb54176bf7eb29e2b9e97cb218): 160 distinct source recording IDs, 25/52/47 disjoint teaching/dev/test speakers. ning, seda, eesti, siis. Unlabelled-calibrated dense scores 6+6,12+12,13+12,14+13 versus scratch 5+5,12+12,13+12,14+11. Neither passed both >=14/16 blocks by 8 examples/word; no saving identifiable. All other tested arms also unreached. Source scale had no Estonian recordings. Frozen plan, raw predictions and controls under mswc-et/.

Estonian extension after original dose ceiling: kept the former 8 lessons per word, then added up to 16 and 32 by the same metadata-only speaker balancing. 320 unique sentence recording IDs across the combined plan. Two new 16-clip probe blocks at each added dose. Frozen unlabelled dense reader scored 12+14 at 16 and 13+11 at 32; scratch 9+14 and 10+11. No mastery crossing in either arm. Evaluator-only fixed 64-probe fork: dense reader got 49, 50, 46 correct with 8, 16 and 32 lessons per word respectively. Further examples alone did not improve this matcher consistently. Raw data in mswc-et/*extended*.json.

Estonian evidence aggregation: per candidate word, average its three smallest acoustic distances from distinct teaching speakers; compare to its single smallest distance. Identical cached reference waveforms and DTW measurements. On original 64 diagnostic probes nearest vs three voices gave 49/50, 50/49, 46/49 correct at doses 8,16,32; 3/8 previously degraded probes rescued at 32. Froze 64 additional distinct source recordings using same speaker partitions, teaching unchanged. Fresh nearest vs three: 52/54, 44/50, 48/50. At 32, three voices rescued 3/7 cases lost by nearest between 8 and 32. Scope: diagnosis of pooling on the same four words, not an independent language acquisition curve.

Estonian edge audit: all 384 clips so far are exactly one second. Before opening another 64 clips, fix threshold at 1% of peak frame power (same as source calibration); retain all interior frames between first and last passing windows. Predict improved 32-example nearest-exemplar accuracy versus untrimmed waveforms on fresh probes; include the equally trimmed scratch reader. No target alignment or labels used to trim.

Fresh Estonian 64-recording confirmation: at doses 8/16/32 nearest untrimmed voicing scored 58/54/53; trimmed voicing 58/59/58; trimmed scratch 58/57/56. Three-speaker pooling at 32 scored 59 for either voicing input and 60 for trimmed scratch. Edge handling accounts for some nearest-exemplar degradation; these same-probe forks do not measure examples saved. Results in mswc-et/*edge-confirm*.json.

Preregistered follow-up on the next four Estonian keywords by metadata coverage: exclude previous words and sentence recordings. Same 1%-peak edge rule for dense scratch and unlabelled voicing, compare nearest and average of up to three nearest distinct teaching speakers per word. Score 1/2/4/8/16/32 examples per word with two new 16-item blocks per dose; first >=14/16 on each qualifies. Prediction: matched trimming should make the scratch reader competitive.

Matched trimming, second Estonian vocabulary: 320 unique recordings across 81 teaching and 72/65 probe speakers. All six fresh doses completed. Neither reader with either aggregation rule achieved >=14/16 in both blocks. At 16 examples/word nearest voicing 12+13 vs scratch 12+14; at 32 voicing 10+11 vs scratch 10+12. No measurable teaching saving. Raw predictions and frozen placements under mswc-et/*trim-curve*.json.

Estonian quantity feasibility: searched valid pinned MSWC records for spelling pairs differing by duplication of one vowel, required speakers who recorded both forms, chose three best-covered pairs before audio inspection. One hashed recording per form per speaker, rejected same source-recording comparisons. Active word span at 1%-peak power, 20 ms frames and 10 ms hop. Doubled-vowel form longer for 17/20 pole/poole, 18/19 tema/teema and 9/9 kus/kuus; median differences 75,80,90 ms. Cross-speaker nearest-duration ABX with half-credit on ties: 497/760, 522.5/684, 102/144. Choices share recordings; these measure whole-word duration, not segment duration or causal phonological meaning.

Estonian local-duration diagnostic. Fixed early low-band peak width (200–1500 Hz, quarter-peak power) and width divided by active word span. In the same cross-speaker comparisons, whole span / peak width / relative width scored 497/392.5/394.5 of 760 for pole/poole, 522.5/383/388 of 684 for tema/teema, and 102/130/120 of 144 for kus/kuus. The local proxy improved on only one pair. For confirmation use every remaining pole/poole speaker outside all three diagnostic pairs with a distinct recording per form, unchanged metrics, balanced distinct-speaker ABX and a speaker-level paired bootstrap. Predict whole span will outperform early peak width, but miss 90%. Also score a separate task where both forms are available from the new voice and only their duration ordering is needed.

On the frozen disjoint pole/poole confirmation, 25 eligible speakers yielded 1,200 ordered cross-speaker trials. Whole span 71.54% (speaker bootstrap 60.52–83.05%), early width 52.83%, relative width 50.08%. Paired whole-minus-width interval +5.84 to +31.64 points. With both alternatives present from one voice, span ordered the two correctly for 24/25, versus 17/25 for width. Next, use the original 20 reference speakers against all 25 confirmation speakers. Compare duration, duration-normalized spectral and kernel-augmented trajectories, their equal-weight combination with span, and the frozen dense DTW reader. Scale component distances by median non-self reference distances before seeing decisions. With audio trajectories fixed, exchange just the two probe span measurements as an evaluator intervention. The confirmation speakers' duration outcomes have been opened; this is a diagnostic.

Fixed-reference diagnostic. Original 20 pole/poole speakers supplied A and B; 25 independent confirmation speakers supplied X. Across 1,000 trials duration scored 68.1%, duration-normalized spectrum 64.9%, spectrum plus kernel voicing 65.3%, their trajectory plus duration 70.5%, dense augmented DTW 67.4%. Paired two-population speaker bootstrap for combined minus duration: +2.4 points (95% −0.2 to +5.6). Substituting the other word’s duration from the same probe speaker, with the sequence measurements fixed, dropped the combined score to 36.5%. 2,177 real registered voicing calls. This substitution acts on the measured cue, not a synthesized waveform.

Speaker calibration diagnostic prediction: a separate ordinary utterance may carry some information about a speaker's pace. Choose a single common anchor word from metadata maximizing the minimum coverage fraction across the fixed reference and probe cohorts, then total coverage, then alphabetically. Exclude study words, reused sentence recordings and duplicate utterances. For up to three available anchor examples per speaker compare the ratio of word span to median anchor span with raw duration on exactly the same ABX trials and with cyclically reassigned anchors. No target labels select an anchor, coefficient or scoring rule. Test whether separate recordings actually justify assuming consistent pace.

The metadata-selected anchor was kui, with 117 additional recordings covering all 20 reference and 24 of the 25 probe speakers. On 960 ABX trials raw span scored 67.92%, own-anchor normalization 63.44%, and reassigned-anchor normalization 62.08%. Own-anchor minus raw speaker-bootstrap 95% interval −10.94 to +1.67 points. This corpus gives little support to normalizing by pace from a different sentence.

French nasal-vowel IPA diagnostic, fixed before reading scores. The cached French metadata includes both ɔ/ɔ̃ and ɛ/ɛ̃ in human speech. Use supplied corpus intervals of at least 20 ms and keep one speaker entirely on one side of a SHA-256 parity split. Measure marked versus unmarked classification at supplied midpoint conditional on the base vowel being known. Use the frozen eight-band spectrum plus two installed voicing cues and the unlabelled source scale. Compare source-labelled same-base and other-base median prototypes, balanced accuracy and per-class totals, with a duration-only control. A 90% per-base target applies. Cross-base transfer above chance would motivate a separately held-out corpus test; failure distinguishes same-base phonetic discrimination from a reusable interpretation of the nasal mark. No manual boundary, airflow or articulatory reference is available.

French corpus-mark diagnostic. Source 252 marked or unmarked intervals from 24 speakers, test 223 from 28 other speakers. Same-base acoustic accuracy balanced across marks: ɛ 85.65% (95/111 oral, 30/35 nasal), ɔ 60.78% (33/50, 15/27). Learning the mark on the other base gave 25.02% and 50.04%; duration-only cross-base gave 64.85% and 64.93%. Classification uses the corpus alignment, known vowel base and inventory annotations; it does not determine nasal airflow. To localize the transfer failure without choosing a new threshold on test labels, compare ranking the nasal item above the oral one for all within-speaker pairs. If only the distance threshold were misplaced, ranking should survive across bases.

Threshold-free French diagnostic: within each test speaker who produced both categories, compared every available oral–nasal pairing and then weighted speakers equally. Learned on the same base versus learned on the other base: ɛ 95.81% versus 11.23% (184 pairs, 17 speakers); ɔ 70.24% versus 50.68% (75 pairs, 10 speakers). The ordering itself failed to transfer, so moving only the binary decision threshold cannot repair these rankings. Reproducible commands from the phonetic-foundation archive with the core Python environment: set PYTHONPATH to the archive's voicing-install directory and run french_nasal_transfer.py and french_nasal_rank.py. Estonian scripts estonian_length_confirm.py, estonian_length_acoustic.py and estonian_length_pace.py share the archive and its pinned inputs; the acoustic script requires the same kernel environment. No runtime change.

French cross-vowel temporal prediction. Use the already frozen French placements, ten-feature scale and speaker split. Compare the previous midpoint to two acoustic differences (end minus start, and midpoint minus the mean of the edges). Use 20 ms windows at the first and last valid positions within the supplied span. As an interval control use the same three measurements at the midpoint and at ±20 ms independent of vowel length. Predict better cross-base classification than midpoint, with 90% balanced accuracy per base and transfer above chance on both bases required for mastery and preliminary transfer respectively. Freeze the same-base controls and speaker bootstrap. This first cohort is open. No method gets a transcript.

Independent confirmation plan before scoring more recordings. Freeze the three readers and source placements. Use the pinned CV validation split, French only, excluding any speaker ID in archived prior corpus metadata and any previously used recording. Up to two recordings per voice and 50 voices, chosen by deterministic hash before reading phone labels. Include all eligible oral/marked ɛ and ɔ intervals. Estimate balanced accuracy and paired speaker-bootstrap differences relative to the midpoint, with all denominators. If fewer than 20 fresh speakers supply each base, report small-cohort uncertainty explicitly. No fitting on the new placements.

Controlled prosody preregistration. Generate a two-syllable harmonic carrier with independently crossed early/late prominence and rising/falling final contour. Balance complete four-recording sets for 48 unseen simulated voices, with shared nuisance draws within a set. The constructed miniature conventions use prominence or final contour to select an anonymous response. Supply four possible binary rules (two cues × two polarities), a familiar two-syllable layout and two labelled reference recordings from a different voice per deployment. The learner must infer the active rule from two public pointers. After only an agreeing reference both cue rules remain possible. The next, separating recording is identical between histories and the pointer changes. Count unresolved guesses and failed detections explicitly. Primary targets: each acoustic bit >=90%, each miniature convention correct for an entire held-out quartet >=80%. Also test duration-only and amplitude-only prominence generation as cue-removal controls. This tests synthetic stress-like prominence and final intonation; natural linguistic functions remain a separate question.

Amplitude-contract audit before accepting the synthetic result: 176/1,152 generated waveforms in the full reference/probe grid exceeded unit peak (max 1.4942). Apply one fixed gain of 0.5 to all signals including noise and rerun the same placements, retaining the original as a diagnostic. Also render matched no-prominence and flat-final controls and test identical waveforms when the corresponding cue is erased. No change to classifier, lessons or thresholds.

French label-free discrimination fork on the opened validation waveforms. Give A/B from one speaker and X from a different one. Pick a single A, B, X per speaker and category by deterministic hash of utterance ID and interval index, using the same samples for all acoustic readers. Require both categories for each eligible voice, give both X labels equal weight, exclude self-comparisons. Evaluate references with the same vowel quality and with the other quality. Retain the midpoint, acoustic edge changes and fixed-window changes, plus duration alone. Exclude French labels from reader fitting; corpus labels still construct/score trials and supply intervals. Estimate uncertainty by resampling speaker identities jointly across both roles. This is a different test from the source-trained nasal-mark classifier.

French validation confirmation: 100 recordings from 50 previously unused speakers of the pinned validation split, 417 eligible intervals and 3,207 registered feature calls including source. With the other vowel as teacher, midpoint / aligned edge changes / fixed midpoint-offset changes scored 34.9 / 64.2 / 55.1% on ɛ (203 oral, 63 marked) and 43.8 / 52.7 / 58.9% on ɔ (91 oral, 60 marked). For aligned changes, balanced accuracy 95% intervals 57.9–70.1% and 44.5–60.3%; paired change vs midpoint +19.9 to +38.2 points and −0.5 to +17.6 points. Same-base midpoints scored 81.1% and 62.9%. Independent voice confirmation of an asymmetric improvement. All measurements still use corpus time information, including the fixed-window control's midpoint. Frozen placements, waveform provenance, scores and code under french-nasal-fresh* and french-nasal-dynamics-*.

New-voice ABX with a single oral/marked reference pair from one speaker and no fitting on French labels. Held-speaker comparisons use shared recordings. Midpoint and aligned changes: ɛ→ɛ 65.7% and 52.0% (2,112 trials), ɔ→ɔ 53.4% and 51.6% (1,512), ɔ→ɛ 47.3% and 50.6% (1,806), ɛ→ɔ 50.8% and 50.8% (1,806). Speaker bootstrap intervals for cross-base edge changes included 50% in both directions. Across-speaker prototypes taught with multiple examples recovered a distinction in one direction that the single-reference acoustic match did not. This comparison does not isolate the number of examples from the choice of decision rule.

Controlled prosody, after the fixed gain correction: out of 192 crossed recordings (48 new simulated voices), prominence and final pitch direction each correct 192/192 in every cue condition. Changing only the second teaching pointer switched the accepted rule and all four answers were correct in each community for all 48 deployments, including duration-only and level-only prominence. One agreeing example left 96/192 targets ambiguous in each condition; after two examples none. On removing prominence entirely, its score fell to 96/192, with pitch still 192/192. On flattening final pitch, the registered detector returned no direction on all 192, with prominence still 192/192. The consumer supplies the two-syllable layout, acoustic prominence comparison and four possible rules. The kernel measured pitch contour. No active lesson selection or natural-language stress claim from this test. Audio example in prosody-four-way.wav and complete decisions in controlled-prosody-grounding.json and controlled-prosody-erased.json.

Unlabelled temporal representation and target teaching preregistration. Source is the 32 previously frozen recordings across five languages, no phone labels or word boundaries in fitting. Compare a 12-dimensional linear projection learned to vary slowly over 30 ms in active speech versus identically fitted shuffled-order projections, a fixed 12-coefficient mel cepstrum, raw eight spectral bands and installed dense voicing. Same 20 ms windows, 10 ms hop, same 1%-power edge rule and nearest-exemplar DTW for every arm. New projection whitens pooled within-utterance covariance regularized by 1% mean variance before retaining the twelve slowest directions. Freeze these dimensions and scales for every target. No learned language-specific metric. Include the reference with labelled source phones separately. Use archived Serbian, Croatian and two Estonian vocabularies for context. For new MSWC languages use every candidate with >=4 eligible words from a metadata audit of Lithuanian, Indonesian, Greek, Latvian, Romanian and Slovenian. Eligibility: >=4 voices per fold per word, >=16/20/20 distinct parent recordings in train/dev/test, four words by greatest minimum speaker coverage, ties alphabetical, no parent recording overlap. Lithuanian failed even the smaller historical block requirement. Eligible new languages: Indonesian, Greek and Latvian. Doses 1/2/4/8/16 examples per word with two fresh, balanced, 16-clip blocks per dose; >=14 on both to cross. Primary teaching saving >=25% relative to earliest crossing among matched deployable controls, counting unreached cases explicitly, no division by an unreached dose. Report paired uncertainty across test speakers; report source costs separately. Predict temporal order should help relative to shuffled order; fixed cepstra may fully account for any gain over the old eight-band reader. This tests acquisition of word labels on supplied clips.

The frozen ordered projection missed the two-block threshold in all three new languages through 16 examples/word. Greek installed, raw and fixed cepstra first passed at four; Latvian all three at eight; Indonesian no reader passed. Next diagnostic: subtract each clip's mean cepstral vector in both teaching and listening. This removes clip-constant offsets but also loses stable word information. Apply identically to slow, shuffled and fixed-cepstrum readers; retain their original arms. Freeze a second Indonesian, Greek and Latvian four-word vocabulary using the next eligible words, excluding every original word and parent recording. Predict a larger mean-centering benefit for the ordered source projection than for fixed cepstra; compare paired accuracy over all doses and retain the same threshold. This is a new experiment and the original target record stays intact. Probe speakers can recur across vocabularies.

Greek two-example confirmation before opening new audio. The second Greek vocabulary was the only new installation where installed voicing crossed before every unsupervised control on the original block schedule. Its later-dose blocks did not cross. Freeze its teaching set; exclude every source recording from both archived Greek vocabularies and all teaching voices. For αποκρίθηκε, only two eligible speakers remain, both heard in earlier evaluations. Construct two speaker-disjoint probe groups using metadata alone, with eight distinct clips per word per group; split each into two 16-item balanced blocks. Confirmation requires >=14/16 on all four new blocks at two examples/word. Replay other teaching doses and the matched controls on those same 64 clips to distinguish an effect of examples from an effect of which probes were scored. This is a fresh-recording follow-up on the previously selected vocabulary, not a third independent language sample.

Word teaching results. The frozen source fit used 192.096 seconds from 32 recordings, 21 speakers, five languages, 8,570 active frames and 7,249 valid 30 ms frame pairs. The fit was rerun with explicit contractions after the system NumPy matrix kernel emitted floating-point warnings; the accepted fit completed with warnings treated as errors. Three new languages and six four-word vocabularies, with 224 distinct source recordings per placement and no overlap between the two vocabularies within each language. Source and target had no recorded speaker ID overlap. Primary projection never reached 14/16 on both blocks by 16 examples/word. On the first vocabularies the average ordered-minus-shuffled accuracy across doses was 0.0 points in Indonesian (paired speaker 95% interval −9.7 to +9.2), +18.1 in Greek (+10.4 to +23.6), +26.3 in Latvian (+17.7 to +33.8). Fixed cepstra scored higher on average on all three. Removing clip means on new words did not rescue the ordered projection. Installed voicing first crossed at doses unreached/8 in Indonesian, 4/2 in Greek and 8/16 in Latvian. Raw spectrum tied both first-vocabulary crossings; centered fixed cepstra tied Indonesian second at 8, raw tied Latvian second at 16, and the supervised reference tied Greek second at 2. No general ≥25% teaching saving. Earlier Balkan/Estonian frozen placements were also rerun under the new common edge-trimming rule and are separately identified as opened controls.

Greek confirmation, 64 new recordings, nine probe voices distinct from teaching, and two unchanged marked teaching examples per word. Four blocks for the installed reader yielded 14/16, 13/16, 11/16 and 12/16. Correct total 50/64 vs 48 raw, 48 fixed cepstra, 46 scaled spectrum, 52 supervised. Selection-stage 29/32 did not replicate at the specified threshold. Source, raw decisions, paired uncertainty, full-dose confirmation and reproducible commands in the external archive's word-transfer-three-languages.md. Experimental models remain outside the runtime package.

Natural continuous-word pilot preregistration. Pinned gilkeyio/librispeech-alignments 0daa1eb43dda38ee6ce752e785555380e5628f5c, English read speech. Forced word timings are evaluator references, with four short teacher recordings per word cut at reference times; no candidate word intervals, transcripts or test-speaker labels enter the listener. Select four alphabetic words of >=5 characters by speaker coverage in development, counting single occurrences >=200 ms. Choose four distinct teaching voices per word from hash-selected dev-clean speakers. On other dev speakers calibrate per-reader, per-word presence thresholds with up to six same-speaker positive/negative pairs per word. Test-clean is held out; select up to 12 pairs per word, one per voice per word, no shared recordings. Match negative sentence duration as closely as possible on the same voice. Freeze a 20 ms search grid, 0.7/1/1.4 times each teaching duration, 12 equispaced frames per window and mean squared feature distance. Score present and localized (intersection over union >=0.5), false alarms on absent sentences, matched positive-vs-negative ranking, and isolated four-way word identity with evaluator-supplied cuts. Target >=80% joint recall and <=20% false alarms. Compare frozen kernel spectral/voicing, raw spectral, fixed cepstra and ordered-source projection; tune each threshold only on dev balanced joint correctness, ties choose the stricter threshold. Use paired test-speaker uncertainty. English occurred in earlier unlabelled source experience; the new corpus and held-out voices test continuous listening, not unseen-language acquisition.

Continuous LibriSpeech pilot (four words which/about/after/little, 16 teacher clips from 11 voices, 24 calibration pairs from 16 voices, 48 test pairs from 34 other voices). Installed reader recognized 39/48 given reference cuts; best unthresholded search location overlapped >=0.5 in 19/48, calibrated joint detection 2/48, false alarms 9/48. Fixed cepstra joint 9/48, false alarms 6/48. Both search and rejection contribute. Prediction before follow-up: at the same location, requiring two independently taught voices to have unusually low distances relative to the rest of the sentence will improve joint detection over single-template absolute distance. Cross one vs best two, raw vs background-normalized cost. Use common candidate windows (union of teacher lengths at three rates), same paid teaching/calibration data. This normalization uses the complete utterance, so the experiment is offline. Confirm on fresh test-clean recordings with no earlier utterance, same words/teachers/calibration; sample up to 12 same-speaker matched pairs per word. Some test voices recur across experiments. Freeze primary comparison as normalized two vs raw one for installed features. Require >=10 additional percentage points joint recall, <=20% false alarms, and positive paired lower 95% gain for confirmation. Preserve same-information fixed cepstrum controls.

The hard yes/no follow-up missed confirmation: on 48 new matched pairs installed two-voice relative scoring accepted and located 3, with 5 false alarms, versus 1 and 4 for the one-voice absolute rule on the common grid. Before thresholding, 22 vs 19 best spans overlapped the reference. Now test a different deliverable: a bounded ranked list of plausible intervals for a downstream listener to replay. Freeze the two-voice relative scoring from above, greedily retain up to three non-overlapping windows, with no reference to test gold or presence. On a third set of recordings, compare to the exact same windows circularly shifted together through the sentence in 20 ms steps. This control keeps the time and spacing of all suggestions. Prespecify at least a 20-point increase over shifted coverage, a positive speaker-paired lower 95% difference and mean total replay time below 25% of the original positive sentences before shipping this as an interval proposal. An absent utterance can still yield proposals. Count wrong first choices, second/third-choice rescues and spent replay time on negatives. No new binary detection claim.

Continuous word follow-up and release. Second cohort joint recall gain was +4.17 points (speaker bootstrap −4.08 to +12.82), below the +10-point requirement. All 48 had an adequately overlapping candidate before selection. For the bounded replay test, a third disjoint cohort of 48 pairs used 32 voices. Correct ranks 22 first, 5 second, 4 third; 31/48 covered, vs 6.23% for the circular-shift control with matching playback duration and spacing. Gain +58.35 points, 95% +41.95 to +72.23. Mean replay fraction 8.75% on positives, 8.52% on negatives. The kernel operation ranks intervals for later listening; it does not decide word presence. Sound-foundations 0.9.0 commit 0ff727c, 11 package tests passed. A new environment with local core and expert wheels reproduced all 288 returned sample intervals over 96 recordings and all scores within tolerance. Warm p95 14.33 ms from prepared tracks, 242.65 ms with file decoding and feature extraction, 313,475,072 bytes peak RSS. Complete measurements, pinned data and reproducible commands under continuous-words/report.md in the external archive. Frozen confidence policy chose no reads, tying fixed zero exactly. Forced three reads moved joint detections 3→12 and false alarms 0→6 on clean; 0→2 and 5→7 on other. Compared to forced three with shuffled receipts at identical spend, net difference +0.1146 (clean speaker 95% +0.0326 to +0.200) and −0.0521 (other −0.1163 to +0.0109). Value-of-one-read study. Three of 48 out-of-speaker first reads helped and three hurt in calibration. English natural stress results. Source 358 examples, 245 lexical items and 40 voices. ### English-trained lexical stress on Greek, frozen before scoring

Apply the previously fitted English acoustic and half-word readers unchanged to natural MSWC Greek word clips. Limit the reference to words with exactly two separated single vowel letters and exactly one written accent. Exclude words and parent recordings used in the prior Greek word experiment. Derive expected stress from spelling only for evaluation. First reserve all available same-speaker contrasts for άλλα/αλλά, ζήτω/ζητώ and πότε/ποτέ, with one recording per version per speaker and unique parent sentences. On the remaining words, sample up to 96 matched opposite-stress pairs per equal/different-vowel-letter panel, within speaker, up to six voices per word, one example per speaker and word, unique parent sentences throughout. Freeze placements before decoding. Use a fixed 20 ms RMS window, 10 ms hop, 10% peak RMS threshold (1% peak power), retaining complete outer frames. Also score the untrimmed wave as a diagnostic. Primary reader uses two automatic acoustic peaks and the unchanged English coefficients. Compare first, level, duration plus level, and learned halves. Report hits by panel, accent position, joint minimal-pair hits, word/speaker cluster uncertainty, fallback count and costs. Predict above chance on both panels; call 90% mastery only at the existing per-panel target and report sparse minimal-pair support separately. No Greek fitting or phone-time reference.

The frozen English stress reader scored 130/192 on Greek words with different vowel letters (34 voices, 152 words), 50/78 with identical vowel letters (15 voices, 40 words), and 13/24 on same-speaker accent-only word pairs (7 voices, 6 words). Duration plus level scored 145, 53 and 21 respectively. Both words were correct for 3/12 versus 9/12 minimal pairs. Reusing the very same intervals in a post hoc decomposition and keeping only the English duration/level weights also gave 21/24. Removing the final voicing coefficient alone gave 19/24. On the original English cohorts, keeping the two weights won three panels and lost two examples on the fourth. These diagnostics motivate fresh tests of cue reliability; no model selected or fitted on these Greek outcomes. Local first-pass full evaluation included 11,760 installed voicing invocations across both preprocessing conditions and two segmentations. Primary preprocessing comparison and replay saved in the external phonetic-foundation archive, greek-stress/README.md.

At eight Greek stress labels, the selector chose duration/level on 6/32 overlapping histories, improving by +0.45 points (speaker bootstrap −2.26 to +4.02) and zero (−5.36 to +1.56) on the two frozen target blocks. At 32 labels, 26/32 histories chose that rule, but neither block reached 85% with any tested policy in any history. Both fixed rules missed 11/42 and 9/34 of the new recordings; an evaluator picking a correct rule on every disagreement would still fall short. On existing timed English data the same rules missed 27 clean and 25 harder recordings jointly. At least one automatically selected peak fell outside the corresponding annotated vowel on 18 and 13 of those failures. Gold intervals rescued 21 and 10 errors but introduced others. Greek lacks these interval references. Local measurements used 3,650 registered frame readings in 11.95 s for 365 clips. Four-word target study completed locally. At eight labels per word Romanian block scores averaged 93.4/89.6% on 16 probe speakers. The codebook crossed at eight and three matched controls at four; the equal-algorithm target-only control also crossed at eight. ### Does a taught phone sequence buy faster acquisition of new spoken word forms?

Before decoding or scoring, freeze six MSWC four-word placements in Turkish, Maltese and Kyrgyz, all absent from codebook and IPA readout fitting. Across a language teaching and test voice pools never overlap; words and parent recordings are disjoint across panels. Each test voice says all four words, and the private A and B blocks have separate voices. Nested 1/2/4/8 demonstrations per word across 32 deterministic orderings; labels are arbitrary response IDs. No target update from hidden probes, which remain fixed across doses.

Primary is square-root softmax of the frozen whole-utterance phonetic readout's 12 phone logits plus background, compared as a time series by identical DTW and nearest teaching example. Match the direct supervised continuous-feature network trained on the same labels, unlabelled codebook, installed spectrum/voicing, raw spectrum, fixed cepstra and equal-algorithm target-only codebook. Separate a compact diagnostic that gets just peak strength and relative time from all twelve registered queries (averaged squared differences, strength divided by 4); a fixed equal-weight fusion of posterior and codebook distances normalized by their median off-diagonal cross-teaching-example scores at each dose; and a frame-order shuffle of the posterior stream. Frozen source readout consumed 8,699 fitted phone intervals, plus 2,876 calibration labels for flagged peaks; unlabelled codebook used 192.096 s. Simple and unsupervised arms get equal target demonstrations. Report first tested dose with ≥85% average correctness in both successive private blocks, individual teacher-order crossings, paired resampling of held-out voices and teaching order. Claim ≥25% saving only if both primary and best matched comparison reach criterion and ≥95% of paired resamples support that saving; quantify inability to estimate unreached savings. Confirm on a second panel for any language-wide claim. Report errors within close pairs and effect of frame shuffling, as well as local call costs. No added tuning on these outcomes.

Diagnostic extension before scoring pairwise comparisons: condition on each of the six single-letter-difference pairs in the close panels. Give both references from one held-out voice and query both categories from each different held-out voice, with no teaching names or updates. Use the same frozen 13-way phone trajectories, unlabelled codebook and fixed cepstrum. Compare full, first half, last half of the frame sequence in reference and query; evaluate frame counts as a separate cue. Predict only an orientation effect for word-initial and word-final substitutions: retaining the spelling-matched end of difference should outperform retaining its opposite; internal substitutions are descriptive only. The half-clips are proportional portions of the acoustic activity and not known phone boundaries. Compare dependence-aware intervals by resampling speaker identities on both sides, retaining ordered pairs, report absolute 90% separately. Conditional four-word errors, A/B/X pairwise performance and orientation are different estimands. This diagnosis cannot rescue a failed teaching claim.

New word-form tests used 942 natural recordings. Normalizing MSWC parent IDs exposed three sentence reuses from occurrence suffixes; two Maltese clips and one Kyrgyz clip were replaced by deterministic coverage rules, including one substitute teaching voice, and affected measurements and analyses reran. Core teaching result unchanged: at 8 per word the scored phonetic sequence hit 89.6/87.2% on ordinary Turkish, earlier spectrum/voicing crossed at 4, and no arm reached both blocks on the other five vocabularies. All six lost accuracy to independent within-clip shuffling. Full-clip cross-voice matches on spelling neighbors ranged from 53.9% Turkish bin/bir to 82.5% Maltese dan/din. None hit 90%; no half-word orientation effect had a positive lower interval. New optional track-phones operation committed at nca-acoustic-codebook f97749a, 0.3.0. ### Buying a grounded demonstration on a familiar natural-recording panel

Freeze the six spelling-neighbor pairs of the existing three MSWC close panels as known regression audio, paired with artificial split/merge conventions. Supply two anonymous contrast menus, eight anonymous named-form exemplars per form (first eight teaching rows, no test voices), one grounded anchor per menu, and public queued counts 6/2 or 2/6. Each independent fair convention determines whether that menu's second form points to the anchor or another object. Public recordings and object display are identical across four worlds. At most one optional demonstration points for the canonical second form of one menu. Fit no new weights. Predict its value as half the queue count times (cross-speaker leave-one-out balanced form accuracy minus one half), using the eight teaching exemplars per form only. Choose the positive highest surplus, stable anonymous-menu tie order. Cross prices 0.15 and 2 correct-output units, charge 0.02 per exemplar and 0.20 per initial anchor pointer to every deployment. Compare never buying, always buying for busiest menu, uniformly buying, busiest only when affordable for perfect ears, independent unlabelled-codebook distance, and a known-form ceiling. Evaluate all four worlds, both queues and both prices across distinct test voices, held-out feedback unavailable. Primary economics: at least +0.02 net/output over the best cheap policy with paired lower 95% voice bootstrap above zero per language. Independently require 80% joint correctness on variant outputs across split and merge per menu with a forced truthful demonstration. Intervene with withheld and alternate valid pointers at the same fee.
