Fit on 16 kHz signal measurements (spectral energy distribution, periodicity, onset measurements and duration); compare duration alone, installed broad phone probabilities, learned cue with all intervals resampled to the same 120 ms at training and test, and a within-pair source-label shuffle. Test forced rank of two matched tokens, balanced independent label recognition and both independently correct. Credit robust discrimination for a mark only with >=90% paired ordering, >=80% independent label accuracy, at least six languages with three or more pairs, and lower language-bootstrap ordering bound >=80%. Report unsupported marks and stricter neighbor-matched results separately. An elicited isolated word and timing supplied by an auditor do not establish continuous-speech transcription or which distinctions are phonemic. Assess legacy 12/44-symbol readouts independently on corpus-aligned intervals so source inventory gaps are visible.

Companion audited naming test frozen before fitting: audit the literal original corpus token separately, then make an explicit restricted inventory of one lowercase base letter plus zero or one of the nine named marks (NFD normalization). These 21,541 eligible intervals cover 95 languages; no base symbol or mark is supplied at prediction time. Hold out languages by sorting all 95 hashed names into five interleaved folds. Use exactly the same examples to train an atomic symbol head, separate base and mark heads on the same acoustic input, and a shrinkage additive acoustic prototype that can generate unseen base/mark combinations. Compare a frozen unsupervised acoustic-codebook plus transparent temporal/spectral measurements against learned-from-raw measurements alone; score a pretrained broad supervised reader directly outside this comparison. Use the same small MLP and 700 updates per fold for the atomic vs compositional readouts, trained from scratch with all three heads on their shared representation. Score exact symbol, base, and mark, language-balanced and pooled; independently report seen symbols, source-unseen combinations whose base and mark each occur in source training, and labels with an unseen component. Matched zero-target evidence; include a marked/unmarked within-base diagnostic, never a live base hint. Require ≥70% language-balanced exact on the full restricted panel for an operational naming claim and ≥40% exact on novel component combinations plus ≥10 points over the additive control among at least six evaluation languages for productive IPA composition. Human interval cuts, platform transcription conventions, word lists, unequal numbers of voices and limited diacritic testing constrain the claim. No commercial release of VoxAngeles-derived weights.

The restricted five-fold naming readout achieved 40.5% language-balanced exact (21,541 audited tokens in 95 held-out languages); 3.3% on marked tokens and 0 exact among 195 novel base/mark combinations in 31 languages. In the separate same-base two-choice experiment, length and nasalization ranked correctly at 84.3% and 72.2% on qualifying languages. Diagnose whether mark omission is a prior/threshold error or insufficient acoustic separation. Keep the five language folds, but for each test fold hold out the next fold for source-only calibration and fit on the other three. Compare identical initializations and 700 updates under natural token sampling versus an equal mixture of natural examples and balanced draws across observed nonempty marks. Both heads see equal update counts. Give each arm the same scalar marked-versus-unmarked bias menu (–4 through +4, step .5). Choose on disjoint calibration languages for highest correct-mark recall subject to ≤10% false positive marking of truly unmarked phones (include always-plain when infeasible); score that choice on test languages from untouched weights. Report unadjusted and adjusted outcomes, correct mark, incorrect mark, missing mark, exact complete and base-only, both novel and all marked, plus the effect of supplying the true base vs the true mark in evaluation-only forks. Crediting marking improvement requires >=10-point correct-mark gain vs naturally sampled unadjusted model, upper language-paired 95% false-positive bound ≤10%, and no more than three points of whole-label macro accuracy loss. Use the prior 40% novel-combination criterion separately. This follow-up revisits the same archive; further independent corpora would be required for external replication.

In the 57-language fit, 19-language calibration, 19-language test rotation, calibrated ordinary training increased language-balanced correct marks from 5.43% to 14.76% (paired +9.33 points, 95% interval +6.42 to +12.82). Its false-mark rate was 8.02% [6.51,9.76], its overall exact-label loss 1.97 points, and no novel combination was read exactly. Equalizing training exposure alone gave 19.48% correct marks but a 13.18% false-mark rate and 5.67-point exact-label loss. None passed all preregistered gates. Priors explain part of omission; the result cannot establish a missing acoustic cue as its sole cause.

Before scoring word transfer from the audited IPA readout, freeze a common ordinary model on the Bengali-excluded fold for all four existing frozen teaching panels. Use the same three source folds used in the bias comparison, natural token sampling and no target fitting. Slide an 80 ms interval at a 40 ms hop over the provided word, using actual audio without target phone boundaries. Primary embedding is the unit-normalized penultimate layer; compare base-plus-mark probabilities, source-standardized inputs, and equal-update control trained on the same inputs with jointly permuted source symbol labels. Compare all earlier applicable word controls including the temporal-frame reader. Hold anonymous menus, nearest-example temporal alignment, sixteen target teaching orders and teacher/test partitions fixed. Report first dose reaching 85% on both groups, absolute accuracy on each, total labelled exposure and registered service timing. A 25% dose saving requires a finite attained reference and bootstrap support of at least 95% against the fastest matched rival. On reused small panels report exploratory scope and disaggregate two-person Sanzhi. A change of corpus or loss cannot by itself establish fewer demonstrations.

The audited-word transfer trained on 12,824 aligned phone intervals from 57 languages. On earlier Sanzhi and the new Bengali take the hidden representation reached 85% on both groups at three demonstrations per word; scrambled-label fits took six and nine. Prior temporal-frame reading took one on each. Neither new Sanzhi nor the four Nǁng action words crossed. Language-macro success on IPA guessing and target word-detection savings therefore remain distinct.

Freeze a label-independent boundary experiment. From source sentence waveforms and their annotated phone onsets (with phone identities discarded), fit a temporal predictor of whether the nearest start lies in each of nine 10-ms offset bins or outside a 40-ms neighborhood. Give its serving operation an onset-confidence curve derived by combining the offset predictions for each instant. Train on the prior expanded source split; tune peak threshold and minimum spacing on source calibration only. Compare normalized spectral change, regular grid at the same predicted count, matched-count spectral peaks, and a prior independently trained phonetic label-change estimate. On the frozen, previously studied Spanish, Italian and Kinyarwanda sentence cohorts score one-to-one onset agreements within 20 ms, precision/recall/F1 and 95% speaker-paired uncertainty, including unreachable onsets outside the automatically retained speech span in recall. Credit useful localization only for >=5 points of F1 over the stronger count-matched control with positive lower bound in each language. On a separate external annotation source use one hash-selected recorded word per available language with at least four audited phone spans, with no tuning on corpus recordings. Match all start predictions to all annotated onsets including word onset (empty outputs valid). Separately evaluate transfer to words with no internal timing given: retain uncertain alternatives by using three source-fixed confidence thresholds around the chosen value, compare their averaged normalized posterior distances against a single cut partition and count-matched equally spaced partitions using the same fixed phone reader. Test word comprehension on the four frozen teaching panels, holding demonstrated word boundaries fixed. If no teaching savings, report independently which stages transfer. Measure whole-waveform operation and leave fitting/calibration/test states separate.

Before opening the boundary test results, also freeze the link to IPA identification. Use the existing broad temporal-frame posteriors unchanged, mean probability within each inferred span, omit blank-winning spans and preserve repeated labels from distinct spans. Use a midpoint as predicted sound time. Compare partitions from learned onsets with a count-matched uniform grid, count-matched spectral peaks, existing frame decoding, the previously strongest small reader, and a diagnostic allowed the true phone intervals but no reference phone names. Include all original references in edit distance and timed-hit counts. Preserve the earlier <=60% full error and >=5-point gain criteria for claiming improved transcription; distinguish a useful boundary detector from a successful whole-utterance reader.

On the 113 Spanish, 104 Italian and 90 Kinyarwanda sentence panels the timing-only learner reached 74.6%, 74.2% and 63.4% 20-ms onset F1. Strongest count-matched phone-change controls reached 73.5%, 70.5% and 61.4%. Speaker-paired gains were positive but below five points in each. On one human-audited word in each of 92 eligible languages, learned 61.5% versus phone-change 62.2%. Holding the reader fixed and replacing inferred cuts with corpus reference intervals lowered full phone errors from 78.6/75.5/80.0% to 70.9/66.6/70.8%. Uncertain partitions reached the earlier Sanzhi and Bengali comprehension thresholds at two demonstrations/form, versus one for both count-matched grids and the earlier temporal reader; other panels missed. The result distinguishes useful boundary evidence from successful phonetic identification and vocabulary savings. Fresh local waveform restore also reproduced 442 audited-interval readings across all 95 languages plus the three complete illustrative nasal-vowel comparisons. The new local 30-second listening replay includes a correct and a reversed Lakota comparison.

Post-score true-interval diagnosis: wrong in-inventory labels won 3,045/5,386 Spanish, 2,808/4,872 Italian and 2,076/3,339 Kinyarwanda sounds. Outside-inventory counts were only 574/255/55. Spanish /a,e,o/ alone were heard as schwa 584 times; the same three errors accounted for 571 Italian sounds. Kinyarwanda /a/ was often read as /ɑ/ or /ə/.

Freeze a bounded follow-up on these opened corpora. Can a small number of target vowel examples repair vowel identity on different speakers and improve open sentence transcription? Use the same frozen frame model, audio-only per-frame phone posteriors, previously fixed acoustic boundary detector, and a supplied teaching menu /a e i o u/ for all languages. Hold out a seeded one-third of speakers for teaching, the rest for scoring. For doses one, four and eight per vowel, enroll hash-ordered corpus-cut examples round-robin across teaching voices. All comparator arms see the same 5/20/40 teaching intervals. At test give the five named vowels and their five fixed source competitors /ə ɑ ɛ ɔ ɪ/ as one acoustic family defined in advance; include every other original symbol and blank in the decision. Only reassign probability inside that fixed family. Compare frozen full model, class-list-only competitor suppression/redistribution within the family, a log-posterior prototype based on true joint sound-label receipts, same examples with cyclically displaced labels, and a capacity-matched donor reader trained on source examples. Use source prior probability among the five as a half-weight log opinion when combining with prototype cosine similarities (fixed similarity scale 12). Keep probability mass outside the ten-label family invariant. Restore original frame alone at dose zero. At the primary eight-per-vowel endpoint require +10 points on the five eligible reference vowels versus the stronger class-list/donor control and >=3-point full phone-error improvement over that same control in each language, with lower paired speaker bounds positive; require <=3-point harm on other sounds. Report naturally occurring non-menu vowels, actual anchors and voices, growing-dose curves, causal label-shuffle and gains missed when only word-level or unlabelled feedback is available. Treat these as privileged acoustic demonstrations, distinct from free exposure or discovering the community's inventory. This is a development follow-up; no tuning on test speakers and no novel-language claim.

The true-target eight-per-vowel readout identified the five target vowels on 1,027/1,546 Spanish, 998/1,577 Italian and 519/1,047 Kinyarwanda aligned intervals in held-out speakers. The explicit inventory alone lifted the respective 32.0/33.5/29.3% original rates to 60.9/59.2/53.0%; matched donor anchors reached 63.2/62.0/57.0%. Target anchors reached 66.4/63.3/49.6%. Full-utterance errors on inferred cuts with target anchors were 65.0/63.2/74.6%, versus 66.1/63.7/70.9% using donor anchors. None reached the prespecified meaningful gains. Direct label correspondence mattered under replay, but target receipts did worse than donor examples on Kinyarwanda. Anchor and test identities were verified disjoint in all three cohorts. The supplied list of allowable replacements was the main source of the large accuracy rise versus the frozen reader; independent discovery of that list is still untested in this study.

### Inferring sound frequencies without a supplied target inventory

Freeze a source-community transfer test after the five-vowel experiment. Use the existing 44-symbol and blank frame sensor plus a frozen acoustic boundary predictor. No vowel subset or target language ID enters the new reader. Learn a library of sound-frequency profiles from the manually annotated VoxAngeles field words, keeping frequency estimation separate from the fitted acoustic classifier. Reserve every third hash-ordered language for evaluation; learn profiles only from the others. Exclude duplicate waveforms and keep all words of a language together. Score the 32 new-profile languages separately from the prior Spanish, Italian and Kinyarwanda sentence controls. For the archive require at least 12 separate words for at most eight exposure words plus at least four test words; reported coverage conditional on availability. Retain the previously fixed disjoint teaching/test speakers for sentences; expose at most eight ordinary unlabelled recordings from different teaching voices. Charge exposure duration and actual paid phone answers. Source IPA frequency estimation uses only exact NFC matches to known broad labels, without assigning unfamiliar symbols an invented broad equivalent; account for all such targets in edit distance.

Compare frozen acoustics, a single cross-language prior learned without target examples, local acoustic frequency estimates, and retrieval of similar source-community profiles from the same unlabelled audio. Use the source language-weighted soft acoustic histogram as the reference, half-count smoothing, square-root histograms for acoustic matching, effective support extending at least to the fifth nearest donor, and share models/decoder between methods. Optionally ask for the phone at a predicted segment midpoint; choose queries by expected information about which source profile applies. Compare random equally charged midpoints and simple estimating of frequencies from those labels. Test zero, two and eight answers. Mask or permute paid replies after selection holding the true branch's queries fixed. Test mismatched passive exposure with equal recording count and report duration. A post hoc full target profile is an evaluator-only diagnostic. Predeclare a three-point reduction in full error against the better frozen/universal control with positive paired 95% lower bound in each sentence language and pooled held-out field languages, plus improvement on the earlier five-vowel interval probe without more than three points of other-sound harm. A gain over root acoustics alone is not acquisition if a universal correction explains it. Paid inquiry must independently beat matched random by two error points to warrant the additional claim. Report direct target teaching separately from previously incurred source cost. Do not promote code or tune on held-out results to rescue a missed criterion.

With no named target inventory, the universal correction learned on 15,233 source intervals (11,418 exact known names) reduced sentence phone error from 77.9/74.9/81.3% to 66.5/65.1/73.9%. Native unlabelled-profile retrieval gave 69.8/67.0/74.1%. In 32 held-out archive languages universal 83.9% vs passive 84.7%, weighted by phone count. The primary acquisition threshold failed. With eight answers, active vs random errors were 66.6 vs 65.9%, 64.5 vs 70.5%, and 75.2 vs 75.8%; archive 84.4 vs 83.5%. This profile likelihood can often ignore sound-label pairing: absent floors and unrecognized labels, multiplying the answer probabilities across fixed requests cancels the acoustic-label alignment from the odds between language priors. A changed sequence of replies with the same histogram can leave the posterior invariant.

Freeze a second study on the same opened placements. Fit 32 anonymous acoustic regions on source-only square-root posterior vectors at inferred segment midpoints. Use source public observations and corresponding audited IPA midpoints to learn global region-specific output distributions. Every source region shrinks toward acoustic scores so all outputs remain possible. Keep unknown named sounds distinct from absence at query time and disclose how out-of-inventory symbols are counted. Learn regional corrections from eight target answers using local region memberships. Compare the same eight examples used as only answer counts, wrong binding via cyclic shifts, no answers, and random-spend. A generic one-step value rule should ask about regions that reappear in ordinary exposure and whose answers can change later decisions; no test audio is used to rank questions. Run at fixed 2/8 doses and compare with both universal source controls from this and the previous study. Hold fitted regions, shrinkage and metrics fixed before evaluation. Primary meaningful effect: >=3 full phone-error points better than the stronger universal control, >=2 over spending-matched random, >=2 over cyclic receipt on the identical paid requests, in the 32-language archive and in each sentence language independently, with paired lower bounds above zero. Report same-histogram invariance violations directly, useful and harmful corrections, and remaining vocabulary acquisition test independently.

Binding the eight answers to local acoustic regions changed 128/153/85 inferred sound readings in the Spanish/Italian/Kinyarwanda cohorts when labels were cyclically displaced at fixed times, and 561 on the held-out field words. On corpus-provided intervals the true assignment repaired 69/55/22 decisions relative to shuffled receipts while breaking 9/26/14. Whole-utterance error after active versus equally paid random selection was 65.55/65.55%, 64.64/64.94%, 73.39/73.16%, and 84.91/83.77% on the 32-language archive. These effects do not meet the declared inquiry and adaptation thresholds. Retain the universal source-only method as a local research comparator, with its corpus-derived parameters subject to the original data terms.

### Does transferable IPA calibration reduce grounding cost on unseen words?

Freeze a new word-level comparison on Welsh and Ukrainian MSWC (MLCommons revision 0bc9df68e92fd6bb54176bf7eb29e2b9e97cb218). Both target languages are outside the previous supervised 63-language calibration bank. Use validated corpus word clips, no phone labels or target inventory. Take the eight well-covered alphabetic forms of at least four letters with greatest minimum distinct-speaker coverage across three seeded disjoint speaker partitions; use four to seven if eight are infeasible. Require 16 independent parent recordings per word to teach and 20 per word on each test partition, with >=4 speakers per partition per selected word. Allocate parent sentence IDs globally exclusively across the entire deployment. Allocate four fresh probes per word per partition at each of doses 1,2,4,8,16; no query recording repeats at later doses. Rotate anonymous pointer handles. For each of 16 seeded teaching schedules use the same bank and a single first-decision nearest-example DTW rule. Compare the primary 63-language universal correction, the same frame reader unchanged, the 32-region source correction, fixed target-only cepstra, frozen unlabelled codebook, installed 12-phone tracks, existing word-labelled projection and spectrum plus voicing. The source phonetic models never see target transcripts or target phone cuts. Compare the first dose attaining 85% on BOTH held-out voice blocks, plus how many later block pairs retain it, paired speaker/schedule bootstrap (>=95% support for >=25% earlier than the fastest attained competitor). Restrict population claims to sampled recordings and disclose supplied cuts and source labels. On the two harder previous field panels, separately test the same fixed corrections without refitting. Do not alter controls based on test predictions. If speakers or words are scarce, report the coverage as observed.

The eight-word panels covered Welsh (106 teaching, 132 and 128 evaluation speakers) and Ukrainian (41 teaching, 55 and 53 evaluation speakers), 448 different source sentences per language. At 16 demonstrations/form universal-calibrated phones scored 68.8/62.5% and 87.5/81.3%; none of the eight comparators reached 85% on both blocks at any dose. Both previous hard field panels missed under the new corrections as well.

Freeze a second stage to test whether prior phonetic learning improves the price of acquiring a new vocabulary when the word comparator is trained to generalize across people. Learn on six source languages, using validated whole-word recordings of unrelated identities from Romanian, Slovenian, Lithuanian, Maltese, Turkish and Kyrgyz, max 32 forms per language and eight distinct speakers per form. No target audio, words, phones, spectra or model selection enter fitting. Positive pairs use different speakers saying a source form; train an eight-way episodic comparison within a single source language. Give each condition the same 64 interpolated acoustic time positions, encoder shape, initialization, 1,200 optimizer updates and batches. Compare eight-way training on log-mel spectra plus the frozen phone posterior sequence against spectra alone and the same architecture with whole-word labels shuffled across audio within source language. Use the same enrolled pointers and choose the nearest taught embedding. Also compare the same frozen 1,200-step embedding with classification by mean enrolled embedding to localize the role of prototype averaging; report prototype controls separately. Do not adjust parameters on the two open target vocabularies. Before evaluation reserve a second disjoint vocabulary in both target languages using the same coverage rule and excluding every previously used parent recording ID, including for teachers. On the reserved forms, compare all eight frozen earlier acoustic methods and the matched spectral and label-shuffled training controls. The primary claim is the frozen spectra-plus-phone nearest-example reader reaching 85% in both voice blocks at least 25% earlier than the fastest attained comparator with >=95% paired resampling support, separately in both languages. Report exact blocks, failures, source supervision costs and causal limits; shared waveform measurements and separate historical phone-label exposure must stay visible. If the primary criterion fails, independently evaluate mean prototypes, gains relative to source-label shuffle and cross-voice phonetic discrimination. Do not count any word-label effect as unsupervised phone discovery.

Scoring clarification before fitted word-embedding outcomes: include fixed time-normalized spectral and phone vectors with mean prototypes and nearest examples as additional cheap controls. Compare the phonetic-plus-spectral nearest-embedding arm with the earlier acoustic and matched nearest-example arms for the primary point estimate, and report also whether it beats the strongest arm including every prototype control. Use historical English /hVd/ reserved speakers to test cross-voice ABX on iy/uw, ih/iy, eh/ae and oo/uw, using every ordered pair of distinct speakers with the four recordings; measure the 90% criterion per contrast separately. Exclude these recordings from word fitting.

Training 1,200 source-only comparison steps on 1,176 waveform/word pairs from 475 source speaker IDs and 147 forms improved some cross-voice English vowel decisions. It did not meet the preregistered 85% both-block word endpoint at any dose in either first or second Welsh/Ukrainian vocabulary. The 16-example/form nearest embedding gave 65.6/68.8% on second Welsh and 81.2/65.6% on second Ukrainian. Raw model, source supervision, shuffled control, endpoints and named source costs are archived externally.

Feasibility diagnostic before designing active inquiry. On the four opened vocabularies, give ordinary passive teaching labels to a multiclass kernel ridge reader, with or without the phone-trained representations, and test the same held-out speakers. Candidate phonetic views are DTW on raw frame posteriors and their universal correction plus the source-trained phonetic word embedding. Matched spectral controls are supplied fixed cepstra, spectrum-plus-voicing DTW and the equally source-trained spectral word embedding. Each view independently uses exp(-d / median_positive_training_pair_distance). Average kernels uniformly, shrink by 0.1 times identity, learn all eight one-vs-rest label responses jointly and add the mean training response. Single-view kernels and the all-six-view average are diagnostic comparators. No target test labels or future query labels in fitting or normalization. At dose one give each view its available 8 labelled words for normalization. At full 128 labels, repeat on all 320 independent test recordings per vocabulary in addition to the original dose-specific blocks (opened-test diagnostic). A candidate active-learning follow-up is scientifically feasible only if at least one acoustic learner exceeds 85% in EACH full independent speaker block on at least one Welsh or Ukrainian vocabulary; report which languages can support it. Selection of the best by opened test is an upper bound for this fixed suite. No extra labels, corpus searches or prospective teaching-savings claims from this feasibility result.

Feasibility passed in three of four opened vocabularies. With all 128 labels, the equal six-view discriminative reader gave 73.8/78.1% on the first Welsh set, 87.5/86.3% on the second, 90.0/91.3% on the first Ukrainian and 94.4/91.3% on the second, each over all 160 probes per group. At this point both teacher-free and paid selections remain to be tested.

Confirmatory design for a shared pool of ordinary audio. Reserve a third eight-word panel per language, same verified-clip and speaker-coverage rule, excluding every earlier word and parent recording. Enrollment and test speakers stay disjoint within deployments. Initially the teacher points once per class (8 paid); expose the remaining pool up to 128 word clips in total, with no labels or menu restrictions that identify a clip. Count all 128 waveform previews and their durations separately. Freeze the median bandwidths on the unlabelled pool for all competing methods. Fit an equal weighted six-view regularized kernel readout. Split it into a three-view phonetic arm and a matched three-view acoustic-only arm. Include random acquisition and balanced teaching schedules using the same readout. The balanced teacher is allowed to select a requested form; the open-pool chooser never sees corpus word IDs. The active rule picks the unlabelled item giving greatest pool-averaged posterior variance reduction weighted by uncertainty of current guesses. Equal-score ties use a seeded random order. First test the primary six-view active vs six-view passive and matched acoustic-only active; separately test contribution from historical phonetic labels. Run 16 matched initial schedules and total pointer doses 8, 16, 32, 64, 128. Give every dose fresh A/B test items, no test outcomes enter acquisition; full-bank accuracy on all 320 is a separate diagnostic. Require 85% in each of two disjoint voice blocks and >=25% earlier crossing than strongest attained comparator with >=95% paired uncertainty support per language. Matched receipt intervention at total dose 32 cyclically moves the 24 post-initial paid replies between the same chosen clips, preserving their histogram; all other data and costs stay fixed. Preregister 10-point causal accuracy gain over that intervention. Preserve unmet criteria, actual queries and complete learning curves. Keep full-bank reliability and source costs separate from any claim about selective inquiry or mastery.

On the third Welsh and Ukrainian eight-word vocabularies the six-view active recording selector first crossed both 85% blocks at 32 and 16 pointers respectively. Random selection required 64 in both. Balanced teaching tied the active selector on both vocabularies. At 32 paid labels, cyclically moving the last 24 between the same chosen waveforms changed pooled accuracy from 927 to 249 of 1,024 decisions in Welsh and 942 to 238 of 1,024 in Ukrainian. The denominator repeats 64 test recordings across 16 schedules per language. Full-bank accuracy on all 320 test clips per vocabulary was 94.4/92.5% and 98.1/96.9% across the two independent speaker groups.

### Does a cross-speaker word representation locate its grounded target in continuous speech?

Freeze the six-language episodic word networks with and without supervised phonetic inputs, and the shuffled-label network. Evaluate search independently of corpus word cuts using four existing English targets and the same sixteen explicitly cropped teaching examples on new, unused LibriSpeech clean and other test recordings. Use common fixed search windows, starts every 50 ms plus the last admissible start, lengths 0.7/1.0/1.4 times the median duration of the four taught instances of the requested form. Use the measured acoustic frames of each full sentence, interpolate each window to 64 positions, compare it with the same 16 labeled examples in each view. For each window score the requested form against the best other form by the mean distance of the two nearest examples per class. Compare prior phonetic-plus-mel representation, equal-training mel-only, within-language shuffled supervision and fixed acoustic/phone views. Test the same matching rule at evaluator-provided cuts only as a diagnostic. Include four-choice accuracy at the supplied interval, raw grid coverage, top-one and top-three localization at interval IoU >=0.5, correct member of a same-speaker positive/negative pair, and the joint choice plus location. Keep calibrated presence/rejection separate, choosing each threshold on the 24 original calibration pairs by maximum joint positive recall subject to <=3 negative false accepts; break ties by fewer false accepts then stricter threshold. Report false alarms, serving time from waveform, candidate count and source cost. Compare with the existing installed replay operation on the same fresh placements. On each test cohort separately require >=60% joint pair choice plus location and >=10-point advantage over matched spectral-only and the installed comparator with a positive speaker-paired lower 95% bound. Use up to 12 different voices per word per cohort, same-speaker negatives matched in duration, no repeated sentence IDs across tests. Corpus alignments only select and score placements. Source languages of the whole-word representation excluded English; the underlying interval representation includes supervised English. This is a test of hearing a taught form in real connected speech. No general natural-language phonology claim from this comparison.

First clean sentence cohort, before opening the other cohort: the fast comparison of fixed ordered phone scores attained 19/28 joint successes versus 14/28 for the word-trained phone network, 6/28 for its matched spectral network and 5/28 for the installed interval operation. An initial aggregation bug omitted the intersection from the IoU denominator. Corrected it against identical, adjacent and half-overlap intervals before interpreting the localization scores. Raw interval predictions and cohort selection were unchanged.

Freeze a separate four-word replication before source vocabulary selection or evaluation. Take the four most supported naturally occurring forms of five or more letters absent from the previous four, using only the teaching/calibration corpus to order forms by distinct eligible voice coverage and the earlier deterministic tie rules. Exclude all previous corpus placements by recording ID, including this study. Reserve four examples per form from distinct teaching voices, six same-speaker positive/negative calibration pairs per form and up to twelve pairs per word per clean and other test cohort. If a form lacks four teachers after exclusions replace it at selection, before any scoring. All competitors hear the same four demonstrations per form and search the same full recordings. Primary comparator: fixed, source-standardized square-root 44-label plus background trajectories at 64 relative positions, normalized over the candidate, Euclidean two-nearest-per-form margin as above. Secondary controls: the same phone vectors averaged through time (temporal order erased); the ordered phone vectors with time reversed during enrollment only; the fixed standardized mel spectra previously scored; a 12-symbol plus background installed phone reader, square-root scores normalized over a window without fitted target scaling; and the existing installed replay locator. On both cohorts require >=60% joint interval/recording choice, >=10-point gain over the strongest applicable acoustic-only control with a positive paired lower 95% bound, and separately positive gain from preserving temporal order. Score true-interval identities and false alarms separately as before. Report timing, installed reader costs, recording/voice denominators and all losses. These labels are corpus word identities and forced alignments, no new training on the reserved cohorts.

Final held-out first vocabulary: trained phone+mel word embeddings chose the correct sentence and an overlapping interval on 14/28 and 11/48 pairs; matched mel-only 6/28 and 8/48. Only the clean improvement over mel was established. The simpler ordered comparison of frame phone scores reached 19/28 and 20/48.

Four fresh forms in the separately frozen replication were before, never, night and other. Sixteen teaching examples, twenty-four calibration pairs, 46 clean and 48 other test pairs (30 distinct test people per cohort). Ordered frame phone scores jointly selected and located 24/46 and 25/48, compared with 15/46 and 13/48 for fixed spectra, 16/46 and 13/48 for the earlier installed replay locator, and 17/46 and 16/48 for the 12-symbol phone track using the matched comparison. Averaging over time reduced joint success to 15/46 and 10/48; reversing only the teacher template reduced it to 3/46 and 4/48. Paired ordered-minus-spectral gain in percentage points +19.6 [9.8,30.2] and +25.0 [15.2,34.7]; ordered-minus-temporal-mean +19.6 [4.4,35.3] and +31.3 [20.0,42.6]. Both relative contrasts replicated. Both 60% absolute criteria missed. Correct supplied-interval identities 43/46 and 46/48. In 20/22 and 21/23 failed joint decisions the supplied interval sufficed. Single-sentence joint acceptance reached 6/46 and 7/48 positives with 0 false alarms in both negative groups. Every test had a qualifying grid candidate. Raw measurements, paired speaker estimates and independent integer-sample audit in external sentence-word-replica.

Installable acoustic-codebook 0.6.0 exposes the optional broad track, preparation of a taught example and a target-versus-competitors interval search. A fresh installation reproduced all 564 test intervals exactly in sample time from 188 files. Largest score discrepancy 2.99e-7. Under three concurrent replays decoded-waveform to result p95 was 88.1/76.0 ms; file-to-result 131.8/120.7 ms; process peak 298/324 MB. The audio film shows a selected ninth Welsh lesson that turned “gloch” into the correct “gwaith” on another person's recording, then locates “night” and misses “before” in natural English read speech. The English timing references are forced alignments. The Welsh word has supplied cuts and arbitrary board bindings. The external report records all criteria, counts, sources and replication commands.

### Can a taught word be found in a complete field-recorded utterance?

Freeze acoustic-codebook 0.6.0 before field search. Use published DoReCo utterance reference boundaries and all continuous samples between the first and last annotation of each reference. Compare same-speaker, same-file utterances with exactly one occurrence of the target versus a closest-duration utterance with no occurrence of the target anywhere in the word tier. Retain complete single-speaker references of 0.6–15 s with at least two lexical tokens. Exclude overlapping annotation intervals across selected utterances. Keep teacher files and people disjoint from test. Score the earlier four annotated word/gloss pairs in each of Nǁng and Sanzhi Dargwa as a known-vocabulary regression, then a new four-form vocabulary selected by word/gloss support alone. Reserve fresh reference intervals for the second panel. For fresh vocabulary require a lexical gloss (lowercase English text without a leading hyphen) and a single consistently annotated gloss over candidate tokens, select by minimum support across teacher and test people with independent hash ties. Forms/glosses and recorded placements are fixed before any scoring. Freeze up to 4 demonstrations per word across the two teaching speakers, interleaved, and 8 pairs per test speaker per word, constrained by available disjoint utterances. Require coverage or report omissions. The learner receives a target group index and acoustic examples only. No target testing labels enter the search. Diagnose loss into grid, ranking with the target present and rejection of an absent word. Fixed dose is a first portability test; never infer teaching savings from it.

Freeze a separately labelled coverage-limited Nǁng panel. Treat the explicit missing alignment gloss “****” as missing for vocabulary eligibility, still requiring the exact specific gloss for every teaching/test token, and forbid other attested glosses. Use the largest common subset of the four test people supporting four new forms plus both original teachers. Require at least two such test people. Rank eligible subsets by worst per-form support, then deterministic hash. Cases may be scarce after using disjoint complete utterances. Sanzhi's original fresh four-form panel is available.

### Hearing an identical vowel contrast under different lexical bindings

An independent inventory over the published Nǁng word, phone and gloss tiers (no acoustic predictions used) found Saa/sii, glossed “come” on the selected tokens, and ka/ki, glossed “say”/“place”, with transcriptions (s,a)/(s,i)/(k,a)/(k,i). Spellings are lower case in the corpus. The same acoustic vowel opposition may preserve or change this coarse gloss depending on the word. This is evidence about gloss-selected tokens, not evidence of a general allophonic rule; ki has other corpus glosses. Complete test speakers F and G have respectively 29 and 22 selected tokens; enforce disjoint parent files from teachers B and C. Use all qualifying test tokens and report actual counts if the metadata total differs. Other test people lack one of the forms; do not silently pool them into complete tests.

Freeze 32 seeded matched teacher schedules. Each has 3 examples per form sampled without replacement from B/C and interleaved where available. Start every deployment with one pointed saa and one pointed ka. Offer the remaining ten already audible, anonymously ordered recordings without any demonstrated identity. Charge their preview audio. In the corpus-gloss board saa/sii share the first handle, ka uses the second, ki the third. In a matched synthetic board saa takes the first, sii the third, ka/ki the second; same audio, handles and teacher schedules. Neither board identity nor expected label balance is given. Include a no-additional-receipt checkpoint, and fork paid responses between matched boards with question identity fixed. Compare pretrained broad phones against the same classifier on fixed mel, 12-label phonetic evidence, and a whole-word metric where available. Primary learner fits a ridge (0.1) kernel readout between demonstrated clips and opaque pointing responses, scale is the median positive distance from the 12 unlabelled offers. Buy the recording maximizing the available-pool-weighted posterior variance reduction (0.25 temperature, as in the Welsh and Ukrainian study). Compare random and a balanced teacher on all views. Score after each pointer from 2 through 12. Discrimination is a separate no-name ABX using A and B from the same teaching speaker and X from a new test speaker; pair references across vowel within onset, then a separately scored cross-onset condition. Report both conditioned-onset and pooled word decisions. Supervised English etc. source training costs are inherited. Evaluate 90% discrimination separately by onset, 80% both-board correct on each disputed word (sii and ki) and >=85% on each of the two speakers with 25% fewer pointers than the strongest attained comparison. Count success only when each board individually reaches 85% word-balanced correct on each voice; distinct voices are separate probe blocks and schedules reuse recordings. Exchanging all paid replies after the identical anchors measures whether later interpretations depend on that teaching. Separate transferred association from hearing a form, and report how often the classes are right under an evaluator-only perfect form recognition. No target phonetic labels, gold intervals inside the word, or comparator outcomes available to the policy. No extrapolation across a natural language community from two people. Preserve all incomplete conditions.

Word scope results before additional interventions: the primary broad track scored 83.7% for /a/ vs /i/ after /s/ and 84.9% after /k/ in matched-onset cross-speaker ABX. The 12-label and trained word metrics reached 98.8% and 99.1% after /k/ but 79.8% and 79.6% after /s/. No acoustic learner reached the 85% whole-board endpoint. With all 12 pointers the disputed forms were correctly interpreted in both histories on 55.5–65.6% across the four voice/form cells. Exchanging the paid replies on a fixed acoustic path changed mean disputed accuracy by 69.1 points. Perfect form recognition reached both-board mastery after four pointers under active or balanced scheduling. Freeze a bottleneck diagnostic before reading new results: hold the paid broad-phone paths and pointer semantics fixed; first restrict acoustic comparisons to the true corpus consonant or vowel interval without changing the word choices, then separately give the evaluator's true consonant or vowel partition to the classifier at both teaching and test. For hard partitions add independently normalized within-partition acoustic kernels and zero cross-partition similarities; include both correct parts as a ceiling. These are diagnostic privileged forks. Give both onset- and vowel-labelled features the same fees and report site-specific ABX, whole-board accuracy and the two disputed forms separately. Seek a physical acoustic cue only if this identifies room beyond changing the inquiry schedule.

The privileged partition diagnostic changed the next experiment. Holding the exact broad-phone purchase paths and 12 answers fixed, giving the true initial consonant group raised F/G corpus-board and synthetic-board scores to 100/88% and 92/100%. Giving the vowel group instead gave 79/86% and 73/75%. Merely supplying both acoustic intervals gave 78/70% and 70/66%. The comparison warrants testing a source-trained estimate of onset similarity.

### Learning two heard initial sounds with other onsets still possible

Freeze Spanish val-00009 and Italian train-01851, exclude all recording IDs in the prior onset target panels. Use four corpus-labelled initials m/p/n/b crossed with e/o when available. With eight /m/ and eight /p/ pointers, known-action accuracy was 82.3% in Spanish and 84.9% in Italian, and rejection of /b,n/ was 13.0% and 6.9%. Supervised acoustic transfer improved equally class-weighted accuracy over raw onset comparisons by 8.0 and 8.1 percentage points. The teacher points to the same third handle for both negative categories; the learner receives no negative category labels. This is an externally arranged contrastive lesson, not autonomous question discovery. Test feasibility separately with a hindsight scalar cutoff on the original acceptance score, giving maximum known correctness while rejecting >=80% outsiders. Do not use the test cutoff in a live learner.

At twelve pointers, allocating four to /b,n/ examples improved Spanish “neither” from zero to 43.7% but reduced familiar correctness by 19.8 points. Balanced gain +1.3 points [−1.6,+4.4]. In the smaller Italian panel the corresponding net change was −4.7 [−8.4,−0.9]. Even optimally moving the scalar threshold on each already-scored set retained only 22.1%/18.3% known correctness at 80% rejection. Use identical acoustic intervals, memories, draw IDs and trials.

## The reflex-versus-planning test on the architecture's packaged learner

Statement (18:25). The learner in `nca-choices` now carries the picture's adaptive thinking in full. Each visual reader has its own confidence threshold (τ_prob), fitted from matched frozen plays with a price per closer look. The risk of waiting is learned per reader (R_wait), and the risk of acting is 1 − P(h). A finer look is a kernel request that one concept makes as a hypothesis. A fitted two-step lookahead searches ahead only where pressing now and continuing compete. The test is the user's: one frozen learner taught on both tasks should press at once on Quick Press and think longer on the two-press maze. Learners are Codex's 22 November policy exports of the mixed learners (seeds 41300 and 41400, 3.8 MB each, native Mac frames). Fresh scenes: task seed base+300 for Quick Press, base+301 for the maze. 1,800 steps of Quick Press, 3,600 of the maze. Ways: as exported; without the lookahead; without the per-reader thresholds; no closer look; and, for Quick Press, every press held back two steps.

Prediction, both seeds: Quick Press right ≥ 0.95, mean first press at step ≤ 1.5 after the verdict frame, closer looks ≤ 0.03 of steps, searches ≤ 0.01 of steps, and held back two steps ≤ 0.10 right. Maze right ≥ 0.80 with closer looks ≥ 0.40 of steps and searches ≥ 0.20 of steps. Removing the lookahead lowers maze paid-a-step on both seeds, and removing the closer look lowers maze right by ≥ 0.05 on both seeds. Chance all hold: 0.4.

Outcome (18:27): HELD, all ten parts on both seeds. Right share, with paid per step in brackets; looks and searches are per step.

| Seed, task | as exported | no lookahead | no per-reader thresholds | no closer look | held back two |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 41300 Quick Press | 426/445 = 0.957 (0.2367), looks 0.004, searches 0.002, first press at step 1.06 | 0.957 (0.2367) | 424/445 = 0.953, looks 0.012 | 0.957 | 0/358 |
| 41400 Quick Press | 446/452 = 0.987 (0.2478), looks 0.001, searches 0.000, first press at step 1.03 | 0.987 | 0.987, looks 0.007 | 0.987 | 0/362 |
| 41300 maze | 1,048/1,188 = 0.882 (0.2911), looks 0.631, searches 0.343 | 1,019/1,204 = 0.846 (0.2831) | as exported | 579/923 = 0.627 (0.1608) | — |
| 41400 maze | 1,067/1,196 = 0.892 (0.2964), looks 0.639, searches 0.421 | 1,014/1,223 = 0.829 (0.2817) | as exported | 693/1,122 = 0.618 (0.1925) | — |

The same frozen learner presses at the first frame on Quick Press, with a closer look at one step in 250–1,000 and almost no search. On the maze it looks closer at 63–64% of steps and searches two presses ahead at 34–42%. On Quick Press the closer look adds nothing (dropping it leaves 426 and 446 right). On the maze, dropping it costs 0.26–0.27 of the right share, and dropping the lookahead costs 0.036 and 0.063 of the right share and 0.008 and 0.015 paid per step. The per-reader thresholds change no maze decision. On Quick Press they cut closer looks 3- and 7-fold, with right answers unchanged or two more. Held back two steps, no press is paid. Milliseconds per step are not compared, because eight runs shared the machine. The learners are the 22 November mixed-task learners, so this tests the packaged mechanism, not new teaching.

## A listener taught on all the aligned speech at hand

Statement (18:38). Every phonetic reader so far was fitted on little speech: the largest used 112 minutes from 780 speakers, two hidden layers and 1,600 updates. Phone error in held-out languages stayed at 65–80%, and cross-speaker discrimination was near chance for stop voicing and place. The shards already on disk (`codebook-ipa`, `sequence-objective`) hold 30.7 hours of phone-aligned Common Voice sentences from about 1,840 speakers in eight languages. The idea is to remove the starvation before anything else. A speaker has a vocal tract of their own, so a category that survives a change of speaker has to be learned from many speakers saying the same sound in many contexts. One change at a time: the same network and input, fitted on 1.9 hours and on all the source speech.

Frozen before fitting:
- **Held-out languages:** Spanish and Italian, wholly absent from fitting (their 9.5 hours are used for nothing but the test).
- **Source:** Catalan, English, Swahili, Kinyarwanda, Bashkir and French, 21.2 hours from about 1,580 speakers. One source speaker in twenty is kept out as a development set, and every choice of settings is made there.
- **Input:** 40 log-mel bands every 10 ms from the 16 kHz waveform, each band mean- and variance-normalised over its utterance.
- **Network:** convolutions over time with about 150 ms of context on either side, taught to name each frame's aligned phone symbol among the union of source symbols and silence. The representation scored is its last hidden layer.
- **Arms:** the normalised log-mel bands themselves; the network on a random 9% of source utterances (1.9 hours); the network on all source utterances.
- **Test (ABX, no naming):** A and B are two different phones from one speaker, X is one of the two from another speaker, and all three are followed by the same phone. Distance is dynamic time warping over frames with cosine distance, divided by path length. Up to 2,000 triplets a direction for each pair, drawn evenly over contexts and speaker pairs with a fixed seed. A pair needs 200 triplets to count. A family's score is the mean over its pairs.
- **Families and pairs:** voicing (p/b, t/d, k/ɡ, f/v, s/z, t͡ʃ/d͡ʒ); place (p/t, t/k, p/k, m/n, n/ɲ, b/d, d/ɡ, f/s); manner (t/s, d/n, b/m, n/l, l/r or l/ɾ); vowel quality (i/e, e/a, a/o, o/u, i/u); length (Italian only: t/tː, l/lː, s/sː, n/nː, k/kː, p/pː, r/rː). Spanish dental stops count as t and d.
- **Target:** the goal's 90% in each family, in both languages.

Prediction. Log-mel bands: 70–80% in voicing, place and vowels, about 85% in manner, about 60% in length. The 1.9-hour network: about 5 points above the bands. The full network: at least 4 points above the 1.9-hour network in every segmental family in both languages (chance 0.7); mean over the four segmental families at least 86% in both languages (chance 0.6); at least 90% in three of the four in both languages (chance 0.3); length below 85% (chance 0.75), since nothing in the source speech is taught as long against short.

Outcome (19:15): the gain from more speech HELD; the level FAILED. Cross-speaker ABX accuracy, same triplets for every arm, with 95% intervals over X's speakers for the full listener.

| Language, family | log-mel bands | 1.9-hour listener | 23-hour listener |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Spanish voicing | 0.649 | 0.716 | 0.761 [0.740, 0.782] |
| Spanish place | 0.563 | 0.666 | 0.758 [0.744, 0.773] |
| Spanish manner | 0.584 | 0.660 | 0.765 [0.748, 0.780] |
| Spanish vowel quality | 0.619 | 0.712 | 0.774 [0.762, 0.785] |
| Italian voicing | 0.660 | 0.679 | 0.721 [0.697, 0.748] |
| Italian place | 0.582 | 0.651 | 0.765 [0.746, 0.784] |
| Italian manner | 0.604 | 0.711 | 0.769 [0.743, 0.791] |
| Italian vowel quality | 0.642 | 0.725 | 0.782 [0.774, 0.792] |
| Italian length | 0.558 | 0.554 | 0.562 [0.543, 0.582] |

- HELD: the full listener is at least 4 points above the 1.9-hour one in all eight segmental cells (4.2 to 11.3 points), and length stays below 85%.
- FAILED: the mean over the four segmental families is 76.4% in Spanish and 75.9% in Italian, against the 86% predicted; no family reaches 90%.
- FAILED: the bands were predicted at 70–85% and scored 56–66%. With X from the same speaker (a check run after the fact, Spanish only) the same bands score 76–82%, so the loss is the change of speaker and microphone and not a fault in the scoring.
- Fitting: 6,000 updates each, 84 symbols. Frame accuracy on source speakers kept out was 0.602 for the 1.9-hour listener (best at 1,500 updates, then falling) and 0.706 for the full one (still rising at the end). The source set is 23.1 hours with silences counted.
- Best single pairs for the full listener: i/u 0.90 and 0.89, f/s 0.89 in Italian, t/s 0.84 and 0.83. Worst: s/z 0.53 in Italian, m/n 0.67 and 0.72, o/u 0.67 and 0.71, and every length pair (0.51–0.64).

Eleven times the speech bought 5 to 11 points. At that rate more speech alone does not reach 90% with what one machine can fit, and the full listener was still underfitted. The length family is untouched by any arm: nothing here is taught to tell long from short.

Statement (19:18), after reading on the measure. On the standard triphone test of this kind, raw spectra score about 77%, bottleneck features taught on other languages about 86–87%, and a model taught on the test language itself about 92% (Hermann et al. 2018; Feng and Lee 2019). Three checks on the full listener, run on source speakers kept out of fitting: its last hidden layer, its scores before the softmax and the roots of its symbol chances differ by at most 2 points; on Catalan it scores 0.83–0.86 a family, on English 0.61–0.77. So with new speakers of a language it was taught, the listener is itself short of 90%. Its frame accuracy of 0.706 was still rising, and it sees 180 ms either side of a frame, which is too little to tell what kind of voice and microphone it is hearing.

One change: the network. Two convolutions, then two recurrent layers read the whole utterance in both directions, then a linear layer of 64 units, which is the representation scored. Same source speech, same symbols, same 6,000 updates (crops of 3 s, 96 a batch), same test and triplets. Prediction: frame accuracy on source speakers kept out at least 0.76 (chance 0.7); at least 4 points above the first full listener in the mean over the four segmental families in both languages (chance 0.6); a mean of at least 82% in both (chance 0.4); no family at 90% (chance 0.8); length still under 65% (chance 0.85).

Statement (19:21), length. The comparison warps time to align two sounds, so it cannot hear that one lasts longer; every arm scored 0.55–0.56 on Italian long against short consonants. The transparent measurement for this family is how long the phone lasts. Two arms on the same Italian triplets, with nothing fitted: the difference of log durations, and the same after dividing each duration by the mean phone duration of its utterance (the speaker's rate). Durations come from the corpus alignment. Prediction: plain duration 0.68–0.78; rate-corrected at least 2 points above plain (chance 0.6); neither reaches 0.90 (chance 0.8).

Outcome (19:23), length: FAILED, and the fault is in the corpus. Plain duration scored 0.542 and rate-corrected 0.576 on the Italian long-against-short triplets (predicted 0.68–0.78), with t/tː at 0.48 and k/kː at 0.47. The alignment that comes with the corpus gives long stops barely longer intervals than short ones: median 70 ms for tː against 60 ms for t, 80 against 70 for k, 60 against 60 for p, where Italian long stops run near double. The corpus alignment cannot carry a test of stop length. For l, s, n and r a long interval is longer than a short one in 75–93% of random draws, but for l and r that is because the short ones are squeezed.

A second fault in the same alignment: in each language a few phones are nearly always squeezed into one or two 10 ms frames. Share of intervals of 20 ms or less: Italian v 0.95, d 0.91, r 0.87, l 0.72; Catalan ɾ 0.96, d 0.84, n 0.72, ɡ 0.58; Kinyarwanda ɾ 0.96, l 0.94, d 0.93, n 0.83; Spanish ɣ 1.00, ɾ 0.96; Swahili ɡ 0.93; English ʊ 0.79. Their frames are named as the neighbouring phone, in the teaching and in the test alike. Family means over the pairs that have no squeezed phone differ from the means over all pairs by under 2.5 points for every arm, so the squeezed phones do not explain the level.

Statement (19:23), a second test bed. LibriSpeech dev-clean (5.4 hours, 40 speakers, clean read English, aligned with a 30 ms minimum and no squeezed phones) is on disk and no listener was fitted on it. It tests new speakers and a new corpus and microphone in a language the listener was taught, on intervals that can be trusted. Same protocol. Pairs fixed now: voicing p/b, t/d, k/ɡ, f/v, s/z, t͡ʃ/d͡ʒ; place p/t, t/k, p/k, m/n, n/ŋ, b/d, d/ɡ, f/s, s/ʃ; manner t/s, d/n, b/m, n/l, l/ɹ; vowel quality i/ɪ, ɪ/ɛ, ɛ/æ, æ/ɑ, ɑ/ʌ, u/ʊ, i/u. LibriSpeech test-clean stays unopened as a confirmation set. Prediction: bands 0.62–0.72 a family; the 23-hour convolutional listener at least 10 points above the bands in every family (chance 0.7) and a mean of at least 0.80 (chance 0.5); no arm at 0.90 in all four (chance 0.85).

Outcome (19:25), LibriSpeech dev-clean, 40 new speakers: mixed. Bands: voicing 0.654, place 0.619, manner 0.745, vowel 0.637 (predicted 0.62–0.72; manner above). The 1.9-hour listener: 0.668, 0.704, 0.792, 0.687. The 23-hour convolutional listener: 0.714, 0.817, 0.862, 0.748, mean 0.785. FAILED: its mean is under the 0.80 predicted and voicing is only 6.0 points above the bands (10 predicted). HELD: place, manner and vowel are 11 to 20 points above the bands, and no arm reaches 0.90 in all four.

Statement (19:25), the protocol in two stages. The published figures for this corpus (raw spectra near 79% across speakers) come from a comparison in which A, B and X share the phone before and the phone after, and the whole three-phone stretch is compared. Mine fixes only the phone after and compares the single phone, so X's left neighbour is new: that is the goal's later stage, "new contexts". Stage one is added as the standard comparison: A and B from one speaker, X from another, all three with the same phone before and the same phone after, compared over the stretch from the start of the phone before to the end of the phone after. Everything else is unchanged (2,000 triplets a direction, 200 distinct triplets needed, same families). Stage two is the protocol used so far. Prediction for stage one: bands 0.74–0.82 a family on LibriSpeech (chance 0.6); the 23-hour convolutional listener at least 0.86 in mean on LibriSpeech (chance 0.5) and at least 0.82 in mean on Italian (chance 0.5); Spanish will have too few triplets for most pairs, since its speakers have about 30 seconds each (chance 0.7).

Outcome (19:38), stage one: FAILED as predicted, and the reason is which pairs are averaged. With the phone before fixed as well and the three-phone stretch compared:

| Stage one | bands | 23-hour convolutional listener |
|---|---:|---:|
| LibriSpeech voicing / place / manner / vowel | 0.631 / 0.633 / 0.714 / 0.612 | 0.736 / 0.818 / 0.841 / 0.714 (mean 0.777) |
| Italian voicing / place / manner / vowel / length | 0.613 / 0.586 / 0.617 / 0.618 / 0.574 | 0.739 / 0.783 / 0.750 / 0.736 / 0.600 (mean of four 0.752) |
| Spanish voicing / place / manner / vowel | 0.678 / 0.597 / 0.594 / 0.595 | 0.721 / 0.758 / 0.717 / 0.740 |

The bands were predicted at 0.74–0.82 on LibriSpeech and scored 0.61–0.71; the listener was predicted at 0.86 and 0.82 and scored 0.777 and 0.752. Spanish had enough triplets after all. Stage one is no easier than stage two for these families.

A yardstick run after the fact, not a target: 60 pairs drawn at random among LibriSpeech's 30 most frequent phones, stage one, the first 600 triplets a direction. The bands score 0.758 and the 23-hour convolutional listener 0.891. The published across-speaker figures on this kind of test are near 0.79 for cepstra, 0.86–0.87 for bottleneck features taught on other languages, and 0.92 for a model taught on the test language. So the scoring here agrees with the published scale, and the listener stands with the cross-lingual bottlenecks (English is among its source languages, on another corpus). The goal's families are the closest pairs there are, which is why they score 10 to 15 points under the average over all pairs. The 90% in every family is a harder bar than the published topline's average.

Statement (20:33), written three minutes after the fit was started and before any of its output was read. One change to the recurrent listener: a second loss on the 64-unit layer. Each phone token's frames are averaged, and a token should lie nearer, by cosine, to tokens of the same symbol from other utterances in the batch than to tokens of other symbols (a softmax over the batch at temperature 0.1, weight 1 beside the naming loss). The naming loss says what a frame is; this one shapes the space the comparison is made in, across speakers. Same speech, updates and test. Prediction against the recurrent listener without it: at least 3 points more in the mean over the four segmental families on Spanish, Italian and LibriSpeech (chance 0.55); voicing gains most on LibriSpeech (chance 0.4); frame accuracy within 1 point either way (chance 0.7); no family at 0.90 on Spanish or Italian (chance 0.75).

Outcome (20:42), the recurrent listener: FAILED. Frame accuracy on source speakers kept out rose from 0.706 to 0.756 (0.76 predicted), and the comparison did not improve. Mean over the four segmental families, stage two, same triplets:

| Test | bands | convolutional, last hidden | recurrent, 64-unit layer | recurrent, symbol chances |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Spanish | 0.604 | 0.764 | 0.736 | 0.751 |
| Italian | 0.622 | 0.759 | 0.728 | 0.732 |
| LibriSpeech dev-clean | 0.664 | 0.785 | 0.789 | 0.800 |

The readout of the recurrent listener was chosen on source speakers kept out (Catalan and English), where the roots of its symbol chances scored 0.863 and 0.747 in mean against 0.846 and 0.720 for the 64-unit layer; for the convolutional listener the same readout gives 0.760, 0.751 and 0.775 on the three tests. Italian length stays at 0.55. On the yardstick of random pairs the recurrent listener scores 0.886 against 0.891. Predicted: at least 4 points above the convolutional listener and a mean of 0.82; found: 1 to 3 points below it on the two unheard languages and 0.4 to 1.5 above on English.

Naming frames better did not make the comparison better. A reader of the whole utterance learns more of what follows what in its own languages, and that does not carry to a language it has not heard. A count explains the level. A triplet holds three single phones cut from running speech and is right only when none of the three is misheard. If each is heard rightly with chance r and a mishearing leaves the choice to chance, then 0.76 answers to r near 0.9 and 0.90 to r near 0.96. The bar of 0.90 on the closest pairs asks that a single cut-out phone from an unheard language be told from its nearest neighbour 96 times in 100.

### Does the listener cut the teaching a new word needs? Statement (20:48), choosing the reader on four opened vocabularies

Idea. The goal's flagship asks whether hearing differences speeds up learning what they mean. The archive already holds the test bed: eight-word vocabularies of Welsh and Ukrainian, each with 128 teaching clips and two blocks of 160 clips from people the teaching never used, sixteen balanced teaching orders, and a reader that pools six ways of hearing a clip. No listener of mine has heard Welsh or Ukrainian. If the listener's frames carry phones across speakers, a word pointed at once should be recognised from the next speaker more often, and fewer pointed-at examples should be needed.

Protocol. Each clip is cut to its sounding stretch (within 50 dB of its loudest 10 ms, two steps kept either side), since the corpus pads each word with digital silence to one second. Two clips are compared by dynamic time warping over cosine distances between frames, divided by the path length. Every reader uses the archive reader's own rule, so only the hearing differs: distances become likenesses scaled by the taught clips' median, views are averaged, and a ridge fit (0.1) maps likeness to the word pointed at. Examples arrive in a schedule's balanced order; after every eighth the reader answers both blocks in full; the words are learned at the first count where both blocks reach 85%, and a schedule that never gets there counts as 136. Readers: the six archive views (the strongest existing reader), the frequency bands alone, the listener taught on 23 hours alone (last hidden layer), and the six views with the listener added as a seventh. The first and second vocabularies of each language (four deployments, already opened by the archive's own work) choose the listener's readout and whether it stands alone or joins the six views. The third vocabularies are answered once with that choice.

Predictions for the four opened vocabularies:
1. With all 128 examples the listener alone answers at least 90% in the lower block in three of four (chance 0.55).
2. At 16 examples the listener alone is at least 10 points above the bands in the lower block in all four (0.75).
3. The listener alone needs fewer examples (median over schedules) than the six views in three of four (0.4).
4. The six views with the listener added need at least 25% fewer examples than the six views alone in two of four (0.35).

Outcome on the four opened vocabularies (20:53). The first rule I wrote scaled each view by the taught clips alone and left the likeness matrix as it came; a single view then got worse as examples were added (the bands fell from 0.45 at 64 examples to 0.39 at 128), because a likeness built from warped distances is not positive semi-definite. I replaced it with the rule the archive's last reader uses: scale by the whole teaching pool, average, and project onto the positive semi-definite matrices. My copy returns the archive's published lower-block answers at 128 examples (73.8, 86.3, 90.0, 91.3%). Under that rule, median examples needed over sixteen schedules (136 = never), and lower block at 128 examples:

| Reader | Welsh 1 | Welsh 2 | Ukrainian 1 | Ukrainian 2 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| bands alone | never, 0.544 | never, 0.581 | never, 0.725 | never, 0.706 |
| three acoustic views of the archive | never, 0.656 | 128, 0.844 | 96, 0.863 | 84, 0.844 |
| six views of the archive (strongest existing reader) | never, 0.738 | 84, 0.863 | 52, 0.900 | 48, 0.912 |
| listener alone, convolutional | never, 0.662 | never, 0.794 | 32, 0.900 | 80, 0.856 |
| listener alone, recurrent | never, 0.694 | never, 0.775 | 40, 0.906 | 84, 0.844 |
| six views + convolutional listener, counted once | never, 0.756 | 72, 0.875 | 32, 0.925 | 32, 0.912 |
| six views + convolutional listener, counted thrice | never, 0.787 | 64, 0.875 | 24, 0.931 | 24, 0.906 |
| six views + recurrent listener, counted thrice | never, 0.825 | 48, 0.894 | 24, 0.956 | 24, 0.938 |
| three acoustic views + recurrent listener, counted thrice | never, 0.794 | 68, 0.869 | 24, 0.950 | 32, 0.919 |

1. FAILED: the listener alone reaches 90% in the lower block with 128 examples in one of four, not three.
2. HELD: at 16 examples the listener alone is 11 to 15 points above the bands in all four.
3. FAILED: the listener alone needs fewer examples than the six views in one of four.
4. HELD: with the listener added once the six views need 14%, 38% and 33% fewer examples in the three vocabularies any reader learns; counted thrice, the recurrent listener gives 43%, 54% and 50% by medians (means 41% [32, 48], 57% [50, 64], 44% [36, 52]; intervals resample the sixteen schedules, which share one teaching pool and the same test clips, so they speak for the order of teaching and not for other words or people). It needs fewer examples in 47 of 48 schedules and never more.

The listener is not a better reader of words than the pooled archive reader, and it carries something the six views lack. The first Welsh vocabulary (beth, ddim, oedd, bydd, wedi, roedd, mynd, angen) is learned by no reader.

Choice for the untouched vocabularies, from the table: the six views with the recurrent listener's 64-unit layer counted thrice. Its weight was picked among 1, 3 and 6 and its network among two on these four vocabularies.
